items.title: GTA VI: Console Shortages, Performance Showdowns, $1B More Sales, and Some Tech Issues
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
Grand Theft Auto VI "has caused a worldwide shortage of gaming consoles," reports the Washington Post, with the game only playable on the most recent generation of Microsoft's Xbox (Series X or S) or on PlayStation 5:
In the United States, Sony's higher-end PlayStation 5 Pro was intermittently sold out even before the release, with major retailers out of stock at its $900 retail price and resellers asking as much as $1,900. In Germany, stores such as MediaMarkt and Saturn are sold out of PS5 models and lower-end Xbox ones... Consoles at Sony-recommended prices are similarly hard to find in other European countries, with third-party resellers offering the device at nearly double the price. In Japan, Sony has gone as far as restricting who is allowed to buy the console to block scalpers. The Sony Store sells it only through a lottery open to buyers with a Japanese account and at least 60 hours of verified PS4 or PS5 playtime. 
Windows Central notes Xbox One consoles can also stream GTA 6 from Xbox Cloud Gaming. And they argue that Sony's "Plays best on PS5" tagline for GTA 6 "is a lie, it turns out," citing a comparison from the hardware-reviewing YouTube channel Digital Foundry (which has 1.54 million subscribers):

Digital Foundry's analysis seems to suggest in no uncertain terms that the Xbox Series X version is generally superior to the PS5. Digital Foundry says that the PS5 version suffers from frame rate issues far more frequently than the Xbox Series X... The Xbox Series X version supports VRR, which with a compatible display helps offset frame drops and smooth out performance perception. GTA 6's sandbox is among the most complex in history, so it's an impressive feat that it runs as well as it does in general on both PS5 and Xbox Series X systems... This is without Xbox Series X leveraging FSR 4.1 either, which in theory, could push the visuals on Xbox Series X beyond even that of the extremely expensive PS5 Pro. 
In the end they also acknowledge that "the differences are negligible in reality." But the site TechPowerUp notes recent estimates by Alinea Analytics that PlayStation 5 accounts for 75.7% share of GTA VI sales, or 40 million sales, vs. just 13 million units on Xbox. That's 53 million sales total, representing "an estimated total revenue figure of $4.7 billion... 
"[P]layer statistics show that around 250,000 players have already spent over 100 hours in-game in its first week." 

Meanwhile, The Times of India reports both PS5 and Xbox owners are experiencing console issues that may be related to overheating:

A Polish console repair technician says his workshop has seen a sharp rise in faulty Xbox consoles since GTA 6 came out earlier this month. Xbox is far less common than PlayStation in Poland. Even so, it now accounts for around two of every 10 consoles the shop receives each day. Before GTA 6 came out, it took in roughly 10 Xbox units a month.Owners report overheating, shutdowns mid-session, boot failures and slowdowns. Some machines refuse to install updates or freeze after one. One Series X ran other titles fine but stopped booting after a few days of GTA 6. It now powers on with no video output, then the fan stops and the machine shuts itself off. No common cause has been found yet. Overheating is the main suspect, but Xbox diagnostic tools are limited, so the shop is building its own to read error codes. 

PS5 owners ran into trouble first. One unit that kept switching off mid-session logged 40 Main SoC Access Errors, plus seven APU VRM Power Fail and seven SSD Controller Watchdog errors.
The technician says liquid metal shifting between the chip and heatsink, a known weak spot on older PS5 models, is often to blame... 


A Twitch streamer's PS5 died mid-broadcast while he was riding an ATV through Leonida. The screen froze, artifacts appeared, and the system never booted again, even though there was little dust inside.
Reddit posts tell similar stories. One Series X owner says the console would not power on the morning after a long session, and a dead power supply is suspected. Another managed about 10 minutes of play before a local repair shop blamed the motherboard... 

Neither Microsoft nor Sony has confirmed that GTA 6 is behind the failures.
 


In related news, the social media team at Microsoft-owned GitHub "published and subsequently deleted a bizarrely brazen post on X," reports Kotaku. The tweet pointed to the 58,000 stars earned by a new project launched in August — the PlayStation5 emulator AnyPS5, which it said can be used for "rewriting PS5 executables to run on Windows and Linux. Does changing where games run cross a legal line?"
[T]he video that was contained within GitHub's post highlighted that users' efforts to improve the AnyPS5 emulator were primarily driven by the release of GTA 6. 

The article notes GTA VI's publisher Take Two has been "actively shooting down all of the GitHub repositories attempting to vibe-code a PC port of GTA 6 over the past week."

items.title: Will AI Bots Ever Catch on for Online Shopping?
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
"If you currently use an AI agent that signs in to your account with your credentials, it may no longer be able to connect," American Express told its customers today (according to Slashdot reader Smonster). And ahile Walmart's site welcomes AI agents, there's blocks or limitations on them from Amazon, eBay, Kohl's and United Airlines, CNBC reports. And other sites "have added provisions to their terms of service spelling out that they're not liable if users' AI-driven purchases go wrong..."

The hiccups threaten to stunt the growth of shopping agents by creating a clunky and frustrating experience for users who are just starting to experiment with the tools. The question of who takes the blame when a transaction goes wrong also remains unclear. 

Despite those challenges, analysts remain bullish about agentic commerce's potential. U.S. revenue from agentic commerce could reach up to $1 trillion by 2030, analysts at McKinsey and ICSC forecast in April. Retailers and tech companies are also positioning agents as a helping hand for holiday shopping. Walmart on Tuesday touted its partnership with Meta, saying consumers could "put an AI agent to work" to nab Black Friday deals.... 

For users hoping to turn their online shopping over to AI agents, the experience can be unpredictable. Agents encounter a patchwork of permissions across various websites. Retailers such as Coach and Gap allow AI bots to browse but not check out, while others such as Target sometimes "block shopping agents by accident," according to an audit conducted in August by agent security company Billions Network. Amazon has responded the most aggressively to agents by walling off its site entirely. The company rankled Elon Musk last month after it prevented his Grok Bot from placing orders. In September, the company also blocked Meta's Muse from shopping on its platform, saying it never agreed to participate in the program. And last November, Amazon sued Perplexity, accusing the startup of concealing its Comet agent, which can purchase products on behalf of users. 
Amazon CEO Andy Jassy has said the company expects "over time, to partner with third-party agents," but that any partnerships will require the right "value exchange" between agents and retailers... 
For now, agents remain a niche tool for shopping, with agentic purchases making up just 0.4% of global e-commerce transactions and 0.2% of value, according to Bain & Co. research published earlier this month... But retailers may not be able to ignore them forever. Roughly a quarter of Muse's 10 million users are shopping online via an AI agent with an average spend of $200 per order, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said in October. 
The article notes bots often "get stumped by login requirements at checkout. In some cases, the agents may require human intervention to bypass a Captcha test and continue browsing... 

"A Visa study published earlier this month instructed 22 models from 12 AI labs to carry out a range of shopping tasks, such as buying a TV, a laptop and a hair appliance. The agents failed about 43% of test runs, and in more than half of those failed runs, an agent purchased a product "that did not meet the customer's identified requirements," according to the study..."

items.title: Chinese Data Center Tied to Alice Huang Found Using Nvidia's Powerful AI Chips
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
Friday Nvidia's stock showed a 30.95% drop over the last month, and a 37% drop from its October 2nd high of $239.24. But it managed a 4.83% gain for the week — after some bad news hit Friday morning... 

A Chinese data center with ties to Alice Huang (the suspected Chinese spy-agency asset) "has installed hardware with Nvidia's powerful Blackwell AI chips," writes Gizmodo, citing a Friday morning report from Bloomberg. Those chips are "among Nvidia's most powerful products," writes Bloomberg, and their presence was confirmed by "a serial number specified in documents submitted to Chinese regulators in November," (offering the hardware as collateral for a $14 million loan, according to bank filings seen by Bloomberg News). 
A second Chinese company (this one controlled by a Tokyo-based parent company) also described a server with Nvidia's advanced Blackwell chips in documents for a similar loan in late 2025 from, Bloomberg reports:

The submissions reveal for the first time that Nvidia's Blackwell processors found their way into a Chinese data center that has ties to Alice Huang and Megaspeed. [Alice Huang has ties to "a number of companies" that invested in the second company, and its president is her husband Kang Wei.] 

These processors were until recently Nvidia's most powerful data center products, and they've always been illegal to ship to China without a US license. President Donald Trump has explicitly said he doesn't want these chips — which OpenAI and Anthropic PBC use to train their most cutting-edge models — going to the Asian country, at least for now. Nvidia Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang, meanwhile, once claimed they were too big to smuggle: a standard two-meter-tall GB300 NVL72 server rack, which contains 72 Blackwell Ultra chips and 36 Grace processors, can weigh more than 1,500 kilograms (3,300 pounds) and is about the size of a gigantic fridge... 

Shanghai Shuoyao — the company that procured the GB300 rack and offered it as collateral — is active at the data center linked to Alice Huang and also has significant overlap with Singapore-based Megaspeed, which is under US investigation over concerns that it smuggled Nvidia chips to China, Bloomberg has reported. Shanghai Shuoyao, which hasn't responded to Bloomberg queries over the past year, confirmed this month in a rare public statement that it is one of Megaspeed's service providers, describing the partnership as "limited to ordinary commercial cooperation." 

Megaspeed, meanwhile, used a rendering of the Yangtze River Delta Project in 2024 to describe its largest data center to investors, dubbing the site a "specific area" facility in an unnamed country... The parameters they've outlined in construction plans reviewed by Bloomberg — specifically, the total processing power as compared to the energy input — would be extremely difficult to satisfy with chips from Chinese companies such as Huawei Technologies Co.
 
Bloomberg says Nvidia "has not answered repeated queries," though they add that Nvida "for years insisted that there was no black market for its products." 

The article also notes that Megaspeed (where Alice Huang worked) "won a coveted stamp of approval from Nvidia within four days of its creation" in 2023, and went on to become Nvidia's largest customer in Southeast Asia.

items.title: BASIS Opens First-Round Applications for Card Offering Cashback in the Asset Spent
items.author: Chainwire
items.content:
Victoria, Seychelles, November 27th, 2026/Chainwire/--The returns money differently. Announced today by BASIS DIGITAL INFRASTRUCTURE LTD, the payment card credits cashback in the asset used for each eligible purchase, with Platinum cardholders qualifying for 10% cashback during the introductory Launch Boost period.

For digital asset holders, the principle is straightforward. Spend Bitcoin and receive Bitcoin back. Pay with Ethereum and receive Ethereum back. There are no reward points to redeem or proprietary platform tokens to manage. Cashback is credited in an asset the cardholder already uses, giving everyday spending a direct connection to their digital asset holdings.

The opening of first-round applications marks an expansion of BASIS's existing digital asset infrastructure into everyday payments. Applications are submitted at and close on December 31, 2026, at 23:59 UTC.

Two Card Editions With Different Levels of Benefits

The BASIS Card is available in Standard, finished in matte black composite, and Platinum, produced in metal. Applicants select their preferred edition when submitting their waitlist application, with qualification determined by their active staking position.

Each edition has a separate staking eligibility threshold, as detailed below. BASIS measures the value of the applicant's active staking position against the requirement for their selected tier. The position is assessed at submission and re-checked at the close of the application period.

Participants can therefore review the benefits of each edition alongside its staking requirements before deciding which card to apply for. Final issuance remains subject to the issuing partner's independent review.

Card Fees, Cashback, and Launch Boost Benefits

Both editions feature an introductory Launch Boost period, beginning on the date of card issuance. During this period, cardholders receive enhanced cashback rates, higher monthly reward caps, and additional subscription benefits.

*All monetary figures are expressed in USD. Physical card issuance fees include applicable shipping charges.

Launch Boost runs for three months following issuance, after which each card returns to its respective base benefits. Standard and Platinum also feature rate-lock periods of 12 and 24 months, respectively, subject to the applicable program terms.

Along with cashback, the card program brings together subscription rebates of 50% or 100%, depending on the edition and benefit period, across a catalog of over 80 subscriptions. Travel and additional card benefits include two annual airport lounge visits, a 3 GB eSIM, and one additional card, subject to tier eligibility and applicable terms. Standard cardholders benefit from a 2% FX fee, while Platinum cardholders pay no FX fee during Launch Boost. Both editions provide immediate access to a virtual card upon activation, with Platinum participants also receiving priority and dedicated support.

Paid Back in the Asset You Spent

The defining feature of the BASIS Card is what happens after a purchase. Where conventional reward programs may require cardholders to accumulate points or convert rewards into their preferred currency, BASIS keeps the cashback denomination consistent with the asset spent.

Cashback on eligible settled purchases is credited directly to the cardholder's Funding Wallet. A purchase made using BTC returns BTC, leaving the recipient free to decide how to use the reward.

Cardholders who wish to stake their cashback can do so separately under the platform's ordinary conversion rules. Cashback does not automatically enter an existing staking position, and card rewards remain independent of staking yield.

Submitting a card application also leaves existing staking positions, lock-up periods, Dynamic Reward Rates, boosters, and stToken balances unchanged.

First-Round Applications and Card Issuance

Applications are free and limited to one per account during Round 01. Participants must hold at least USD 1,000 in eligible BASIS wallet value at submission, maintain an account in good standing, and satisfy the staking requirements for their selected card edition.

Once BASIS approves a waitlist application, the applicant receives further instructions and a secure Know Your Customer (KYC) verification link. The issuing partner then conducts its own review, covering identity verification, residency, regional eligibility, sanctions screening, and supporting documentation.

Waitlist approval permits applicants to proceed to the next stage and does not constitute final card approval, activation, or issuance.

is a Seychelles international business company (LEI: 254900IX2F2KCWNSSS64) operating market-neutral yield infrastructure, including execution, risk-management, and settlement systems for digital asset staking.

The company holds ISO/IEC 27001:2022 and ISO/IEC 20000-1:2018 certification, both verifiable through IAF CertSearch.

Base cashback rates are fixed for 12 months on Standard and 24 months on Platinum. Launch Boost rates may be adjusted after the boost period with 30 days' notice. Both are separate from platform staking rewards, which vary with market conditions.

items.title: Mozilla Thanks Users For New Features in Firefox 161: Site-Specific VPN and Keyboard Shortcuts
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
Firefox 161 (released Tuesday) promises "A better Firefox, thanks to you. All of these improvements began with a community request." In a Thanksgiving-themed message, they wrote "Here's to the passionate people who keep us moving forward."




Choose which sites always open with VPN. Our free built-in VPN just got one of its most requested upgrades. Pick sites where the VPN always turns on, and sites where it stays off because they work better without it. Bonus: VPN data is unlimited through January. Use it as much as you like until then... 
Set your own shortcuts . Create keyboard shortcuts for what you use most, like opening tabs, saving pages or closing windows. Type "about:keyboard" in the address bar. 

See images appear as they load. Firefox now supports JPEG XL, an image format that lets you see a preview of the full image before it downloads. 

Neowin notes Firefox is also committing to its redesign:

Mozilla has been trying to win over users from Chromium-based browsers, hoping they pick up Firefox. To do so, aside from still supporting uBlock Origin, the firm made a big design shift this year by introducing Nova, so that users on the other side can feel they are familiar with it, as it brings the more common, modern rounded corner design philosophy, which Google's Chrome has been using for quite a while... However, as is usually the case, not everyone has been on-board with Nova and they are completely fine to feel that way; Mozilla also understands this which is why it offered a way to opt-out of it by tweaking a configuration setting via about:config. However, this week the firm announced that it is going to take that option away. 



In a post on its official Mozilla Connect forum, which was shared with us by Neowin forum member ecmram, the Firefox team confirmed that it will remove the config toggle preference for reverting to the old design next month in December. The company says that the rollout of Nova is now complete, and it wants to lock the preference to ensure that Firefox performs as intended and to prevent unexpected browser behavior. As such, anyone who has previously used the browser.nova.enabled preference to disable the redesign will automatically get Nova starting next month, thus wiping the official way to return to the previous UI once the change takes effect. 


On the positive side, Mozilla is not entirely ignoring feedback from users who are unhappy with the redesign. The company says it has introduced several changes based on community feedback, including a new set of Classic Themes with the latest version 161, that offer flat colors without gradients. These can be found under about:addons, and one of them even mimics the older Proton design with a gray appearance. There is a new Fire toolbar button too that clears history with a single-click.

items.title: Vendor Lock-In Is Creating a Market for Escape
items.author: Chris Gale
items.content:
Jeff Bezos famously said, “Your margin is my opportunity.” Where incumbents carried generous margins and sought rents, a hungry challenger saw room to win by serving customers better and charging less. Today, the line could be, “Your switching costs are my opportunity.” A new wave of enterprises is building a business out of jailbreaking customers from platforms.

And “platform” used to be a positive word. Investors liked platforms. Customers liked them too. And the latter dependably picked a platform over an agglomeration of best-in-class solutions. Our own little outfit is no exception. Maybe you weren’t excited about the platform over the best in class alternative. But the platform application fit with every other platform application better, and the combined cost and security were and remain seductive.

Well, the security may remain seductive. But the pricing is changing.

We have lived this at our own firm. ActiveCampaign notified us that our monthly plan would move from $295.29 to $399.46 on December 19th, an increase of about 35%, with the new rate applying unless we completed cancellation before that date. ActiveCampaign's price increases stem from a multi-year shift from simple email marketing to an all-in-one, AI-powered automation platform.

But putting that aside, its last raise was in 2021, the peak of the zero-interest-rate tech bubble. Venture capital and growth-equity funds like those that put their then-cheap money into the company typically look for an exit within five to seven years. So it’s time to monetize the switching costs developed over that period. Essentially firms like ours whose contacts and CRM intelligence are in the platform. But to the extent that money is being put into improving the platform, it’s not easy to see.

The market is also saturated, and smaller firms like ours require proportionately more handing than large enterprises for less revenue, so we’re no longer welcome unless we’re willing to pay closer to what big companies are seeking to pay. We’re not going to get better service out of this price increase, but large enterprises might.

Anyone who has read about the history of redlining in the U.S. and how places like Harlem paid for America’s suburbs will start to get aspects of the picture, though in an exponentially more insidious and morally corrupt form. Not to pick on ActiveCampaign, because despite their attempting to mollify us by inviting us to pay a little bit less in absolute terms by paying it all in advance, they’ve been accommodating enough about letting us get off here, and us letting them try to focus on the large enterprises.

With Cision - our reporter database and wire service platform - we had stayed through earlier price increases even though the service wasn’t delivering anything new or better that we wanted. We did this because we assumed that in exchange for our loyalty they would help us out if we needed it.

As we’ve pursued a pivot, we asked for help with the cost. They couldn’t give us any, and we gave notice of non-renewal. We then learned that services couldn’t be removed mid-contract and they were bent on holding us down. While previously it was just the reporter database we wanted to address, now we’ve realized that while we saw them as a partner who would reward loyalty, the company is actually a risk and can amplify and compound problems if and when they occur. So we are now moving off both of their services. We’re also looking more carefully at the ownership structure and financing of the tech solutions and platforms we use, because we don’t want our data and workflows in the hands of an outfit that must monetize its switching costs on that same five-to-seven-year clock.

Neither vendor lost us over a feature or poor service. The products were great, exactly what we needed. Though interestingly in both cases once we left the platform we realized we had been missing superior services from competitors or we could just build what we needed internally. It wasn’t a priority to find alternatives, but both companies made it one for us, and we have benefited, as have our own clients.

This is the problem with switching costs as a competitive advantage.

The more a company raises prices, no matter how much it claims the increases fund improvements the customer doesn’t recall asking for, the more the switching costs become a bitter experience. As one operations leader said within earshot of me recently, “I hate platforms, I don’t want us to be on a platform.” And as the cheap money becomes scarce, and U.S. policymaking does that it has been doing in very recent years, that sentiment is likely to increase.

Vertice, a software-procurement firm that tracks what its customers pay, reports preliminary SaaS inflation of 14.3 percent in September 2026, after a record 16.4% in June. Over the same twelve months, US consumer prices rose 3.7 percent according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, CPI release of October 14th. Vertice’s figure is a vendor-published average drawn from its own customer base, not an official statistic. But Microsoft’s own pricing announcement shows the pattern at the largest platform, effective July 1st Microsoft 365 Business Basic rose from $6 to $7 per user per month. That’s 16 percent. Business Standard went from $12.50 to $14 So 12 percent. And Microsoft 365 E3 has gone from $36 to $39 for 8 percent. Existing customers move to the new prices at renewal.

But it’s also the tech talent market

When a software company loses confidence that it can win customers by building better products, it stops trying to keep customers because they love the product. It tries to keep them because they can’t leave.

Challenger, Gray & Christmas counted 171,501 announced US technology job cuts through October 2026. That is up 21 percent from a year earlier and already more than the 154,445 for all of 2025. Layoffs.fyi lists about 149,000 tech employees laid off at 366 companies worldwide so far this year. Companies increasingly say AI is the reason. The evidence for that is thin.

Challenger has tracked AI as the most-cited reason for layoffs for several months running in 2026, but laid-off workers describe something else. In a February 2026 Gallup survey of more than 23,000 US workers, only about 1 percent of those laid off said AI directly caused their job loss. Most cited restructuring, cost-cutting and economic conditions, and that includes a shift away from customer-centrism to rent-raising. A study reported by Fortune in August 2026 foud some of the companies studied cut staff before investing much in AI, allegedly to free up money for it. Revelio Labs found that companies announcing AI-driven layoffs had actually been adding AI talent more slowly than their industry peers, at a median of about 11 percent over two years compared with more than 13 percent. Forrester estimates that only 6 percent of US jobs will be automated by 2030. If AI were doing the work of the people being let go, these numbers would look different.

The layoffs line up better with a change in where companies want their people. Support and product engineering are shrinking. Sales, account management and migration programs are protected or growing. And prices are rising on customers who find it hard to leave.

Start with Broadcom and VMware. VMware had more than 38,000 employees at the start of 2023 and about 16,000 two years later, according to Business Insider. Smaller customers lost direct support and were routed to a distributor, with response times stretching to a week or more. European cloud providers documented price increases of 800 percent to 1,500 percent. Even so, a January 2026 CloudBolt survey of 302 IT decision-makers found that only 4 percent had fully replaced VMware. Untangling the dependencies typically takes 18 to 24 months. The study concluded that Broadcom is deliberately accepting customer churn while maximizing margins on the customers who remain. Support quality was a top concern for 78 percent of respondents, and 85 percent expect further price increases. None of this depends on AI.

Broadcom ran the same playbook after buying CA Technologies in 2018, and Constellation Research analyst Ray Wang said when the VMware layoffs began that this is how Broadcom makes money from its acquisitions.

At Salesforce, CEO Marc Benioff claimed in September 2025 that AI agents had allowed the company to cut its customer support workforce from about 9,000 to 5,000. He says he has held engineering headcount flat at roughly 15,000 for two years. In January 2026 he said the company was hiring 20 percent more account executives. In August 2025, Salesforce raised prices on Enterprise and Unlimited editions of Sales Cloud, Service Cloud and other products by an average of 6 percent, after a 9 percent increase in 2023. AI is harder to accept as the explanation, given that Business Insider reported Agentforce usage remained relatively low and the product hadn’t matched the company’s demos. In early 2026, Salesforce cut roles on the Agentforce team itself.

In May 2026 Cloudflare eliminated more than 1,100 positions, about 20 percent of its workforce, in the same period it reported record quarterly revenue of $639.8 million, up 34 percent. Its executives said AI use had increased more than 600 percent in three months and that employees were running thousands of AI-agent sessions a day. If AI had been driving the decisions, you would expect the heaviest AI users to be protected, but according to reporting on the earnings call, the company protected salespeople carrying revenue quotas instead, and the cuts reached across every other team and geography.

In January 2026 Amazon announced 16,000 corporate job cuts, following 14,000 in October 2025. Washington state filings show the largest category was software development engineers, along with security, data and quality-assurance engineers, applied scientists, UX designers and product managers. Amazon described the cuts as removing layers and bureaucracy. One of those let go was N. Lee Plumb, his team’s head of AI enablement, whom Amazon had flagged as one of the top users of its AI coding tool, Kiro, by his account, only five people in the company used it more. A company replacing people with AI would have little reason to let him go.

SAP’s 2024 restructuring affected about 10,000 roles and cost €3.1 billion. Its CFO said the goal was to decouple expenses from revenue growth. The same year SAP created a board-level unit dedicated to moving customers to the cloud. Mainstream support for its ECC system ends in 2027, and SAP has said future innovation, including AI, will be available only in the cloud. Senior executives surveyed by Constellation Research described its RISE migration program as financial engineering more than a benefit to customers.

Regulators have documented how hard it is for customers to leave. In November 2024 the US Government Accountability Office found that five of six federal agencies it interviewed had run into restrictive vendor licensing practices. Three were required to buy again licenses they already owned in order to run that software in the cloud. One had to pay to regain ownership of its own data when a contract ended. In July 2025 the UK Competition and Markets Authority concluded that switching between cloud providers was extremely rare and that egress fees and licensing practices were hurting competition. It estimated that prices just 5 percent above competitive levels would cost UK customers about £500 million a year in a market of roughly £10.5 billion.

AI gives these companies a forward-looking explanation for cuts that investors reward. The pattern underneath appears more prosaic. Vendors may be cutting the engineers and support staff who understand the customer’s problems. They are putting their headcount and money into the sales teams, migration programs onto platforms with switching costs and contract structures that move customers onto their platforms and keep them there. And they appear to be raising prices on customers whose cost of leaving keeps rising. Customers get less help, pay more and have fewer ways out in this formulation.

Enterprise software used to win by building a better product, solving harder problems and giving customers a reason to renew. Today a vendor can do well by building an ecosystem customers can’t easily leave, cutting the cost of serving them and charging the installed base more. Engineering then gets judged by how efficiently the vendor makes money from the customer’s dependence.

CIOs and CFOs evaluating a cloud migration or AI rollout may want to look past this year’s budget savings and ask whether the vendor’s product, service and flexibility are improving, or whether their company is just becoming more dependent on a vendor that profits from engineered retention more than satisfaction. A vendor that cuts the engineers who understand its users while protecting the people who lock those users in has stopped competing on product, and its customers usually find that out at renewal.

To execute a pivot toward raw infrastructure rent-seeking, corporate leadership almost always chooses a specific archetype of manager we feel, the platform generalist. These leaders’ core competencies are systems integration (without passing the benefit on to customers), horizontal scaling, and cross-application alliances. They don’t see software as a solution that delivers greater benefits to users, they see it as a distribution channel to force consumption of underlying cloud servers.

And if some feature or pricing model will lure the unsophisticated into the trap, this manager is willing to be rewarded for it, trading integrity for short-term margin and a hoped-for getaway when the market catches on.

Under this framework, specialized, domain-rich product teams are systematically trimmed or ignored to fund massive infrastructure buildouts. This creates an organizational environment of intellectual debt, the company stops asking how to innovate to save its users time, and starts asking what the bare minimum is to prevent a total customer revolt.

When a company reaches this stage, it stops creating value and starts extracting rent, it weaponizes its legal departments, licensing audits, and predatory contract bundles to squeeze extra margin out of a captive customer base, and product excellence gives way to operational coercion.

The Cost of Losing the Pro-Customer Engineer

The fatal flaw in the rent-seeking playbook is the assumption that your moats are made of stone, when they are actually made of code and human expertise.

When an organization defunds its application layer to buy database chips, for instance, it inevitably triggers a catastrophic brain drain. The elite domain specialists, the institutional anchors who spent decades perfecting niche compliance features, complex calculation logic, and granular user workflows, realize there is no longer a seat for them at the table. They leave. Sometimes it’s worse: bad strategy leads companies to escort their best people out the door as they pivot away from the user and toward servicing their debt covenants.

Losing a superstar domain specialist is not just an HR headache; it is a structural breach in the corporate moat. Even if the individual is deep inside the org and you think the customers can’t see them, other team members can, and they get the message: caring about the user and customers is not rewarded here, and it’s time to get out while you still can. These specialists you’re losing possess a rare dual capability: they understand the hyper-complex, real-world problems of the industry, and they know exactly where the legacy software’s seams are weak. When an executive lets an elite product leader and engineer walk out the door, they lose their translation shield, and with it the internal credibility required to keep customers from rebelling against an unusable interface.

More importantly, they give the open market a weapon. In the modern cloud landscape, enterprise lock-in is ultimately just a data mapping problem. The moment an elite architect leaves and teaches rival platforms or cloud-flexible competitors how to untangle, translate, and automate the migration of your proprietary code, the “divorce-proof” illusion evaporates.

The One Ring of the Seven Powers

This is where Hamilton Helmer’s book is instructive. He names switching costs as one of the seven sources of durable competitive advantage, and the most deceptive of them. Switching costs are the one ring that rules them all, they make you feel powerful because people are forced to stay with you, even against their will.

But like the ring, the power corrupts the one who wields it. Once you lose your customers’ will, and they must stay with you without choosing you, you have already lost. You are no longer earning loyalty; you are guarding prisoners. And a new wave of enterprises is attacking exactly that vulnerability.

The customer’s side of the trap looks a lot like asking the Mafia for a favor. The first offer is generous: a bundled discount, free migration credits, a deal that solves today’s problem. It feels like a friendship. Only later do you learn the favor was never a transaction; it was a debt, and the debt has no payoff date. Every renewal comes with new terms, and every attempt to leave is met with a reminder of what you owe. You didn’t buy a product; you accepted a relationship you can’t exit.

The more a business or investor falls into its own trap, using switching costs to save itself and squeeze customers and clients, the more hated it becomes. Even those who stay are like the subjects of a Soviet regime, compliant on the surface, waiting for their chance to escape or overthrow it. When that chance arrives, they take it.

This is why switching costs are a toxic, addictive, and self-destructive power to lean into. The more you use it for short-term returns, the more you sacrifice the trust and authenticity on which long-term persistence is best built.

The tragedy of the platform generalist is that financial metrics often shield them from reality until it is too late. Because enterprise data gravity is heavy and moving off a core utility layer is a multi-year, multi-million-dollar risk, revenue may continue to climb for years on forced renewals alone.

Coming back to VMware under Broadcom returns to a test case. Broadcom’s infrastructure software segment, which includes VMware, reported $6.9 billion in revenue in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2025, up 19 percent from a year earlier. AT&T alleged in a 2024 lawsuit that Broadcom proposed a 1,050 percent increase to its annual VMware bill. The case was settled out of court.

Customers have been slow to leave, however. The CloudBolt survey cited earlier, of 302 IT decision-makers at North American companies with at least 1,000 employees, found that 86 percent were actively reducing their VMware footprint even though only 4% had fully migrated off it. That is the illusion in numbers, revenue climbs on forced renewals while customers plan their exit. CloudBolt sells hybrid cloud management software, so treat its survey as indicative rather than definitive.

But a company that takes an anti-customer approach and sells to anti-customer gatekeepers has written its own obituary. It becomes an empire built on quicksand. Modern organizations, the startups, high-growth scale-ups, and developers of the next generation, will avoid these legacy utilities like the plague. They build on open, flexible, product-led architectures designed to remain rent-proof from day one.

The lesson for modern tech leaders may be absolute, infrastructure means nothing if the software on top of it is unusable or beige as one revenue leader in professional services and tech said recently.

If you strip your company of its product-deep soul to fund a commoditized infrastructure floor, you are not building a permanent monopoly. You are handing agile, user-first challengers a highly profitable opening to deliver a clean-break data blueprint and hollow out your captive customer base from the outside. You might win the budget war today, but you have guaranteed your long-term irrelevance.

A simple test, can you say upfront that what you are selling is handcuffs? If, instead, you are selling how cool-looking and comfortable the handcuffs are, you are losing. Your switching costs are someone else’s opportunity, and they are coming for it.

Platform lock-in is now big enough to support its own escape industry.

Nutanix added 3,000 new customers in fiscal 2026, its third straight year at that pace, and much of that growth came from customers leaving VMware. Red Hat stripped the container features out of OpenShift to give VMware users a product that runs only virtual machines. It says the number of VMs running on that platform grew 417 percent in a year and that its services team has assessed more than 1.46 million VMs for migration. HPE became, in Forrester’s words, the first hardware vendor to build its own virtualization software in response to Broadcom’s takeover of VMware.

Many of the people building this escape industry learned the trade inside the platforms customers are now trying to leave. VergeIO, which sells a VMware replacement and recently sped up its migration tools, put former VMware CTO Kit Colbert on its board and hired Parag Patel, a former VMware sales vice president, as CEO. About 19,000 people have left VMware since Broadcom took over. KORE1 says the largest share is landing in the migration practices of system integrators such as Accenture, Deloitte, Kyndryl and HCLTech. A single exit can absorb a team. KORE1 estimates Western Union’s migration of 900 to 1,200 applications needs 30 to 50 engineers. The pattern reaches past VMware. Rimini Street says its primary support engineers average more than 20 years of experience. Dreamteam, founded by former Freshworks executives, has raised $53 million for an AI-native CRM and has already replaced Salesforce at DMS Health.

At the end of the day, where do you invest into your own tech capabilities, both as an individual advancing your career, or as an enterprise leader or investor? The Jailbreak economy is looking promising.

Also, apologies to Thin Lizzy fans for the headline.

items.content:
Welcome to another  feature. Every week, we highlight a standout company from our  that's making waves in the global tech ecosystem and the lives of its users. Our database features everything from S&P giants to rising stars in the Startup scene.

This week, we’re excited to spotlight , a Barcelona and São Paulo-based fintech that offers a single API and dashboard for digital banking, e-wallets, and payments across Latin America. It connects directly to local payment rails, so one integration reaches markets like Brazil and Mexico.

LaFinteca connects global merchants directly to local payment rails across Latin America, cutting out the intermediaries that sit between a checkout and the actual transaction.

The starting point is a straightforward observation: each country in the region runs on its own rules and infrastructure. Pix in Brazil, SPEI in Mexico, PSE in Colombia, they don’t work the same way, and they don’t talk to each other. LaFinteca’s answer is a single API that covers more than 20 local payment methods across 30 markets, so a merchant adding a new country changes a configuration, not a codebase. A sandbox environment lets engineering teams test each market against real payment logic before going live.

The company holds a license from Brazil’s Banco Central do Brasil, the most heavily regulated payments market in the region, and operates under local regulatory frameworks in the other markets it covers. In Brazil, it is also a member of ABFintechs, the national fintech association, which gives it a formal channel with the BCB.

LaFinteca reports over processed to date. The platform runs on direct connections, which means decline reasons and routing decisions reach the merchant rather than stopping at an intermediary.

The company is based in Barcelona and São Paulo and focuses exclusively on B2B cross-border payments.

items.title: Nvidia Seeded Pirated Books and Shared Them With Adobe, Authors Allege
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from TorrentFreak: Several book authors have filed (PDF) an amended complaint accusing Nvidia of seeding pirated books via BitTorrent, after downloading them from shadow libraries including Anna's Archive and LibGen. [...] These tools can download files via BitTorrent, and the authors and Nvidia both agree that whether they also upload data to others depends on the settings used. According to the authors, Nvidia didn't prevent seeding altogether. "When Nvidia ran the BitTorrent client, Nvidia uploaded pieces of pirated book files to third parties during the downloading process (i.e., before the download was complete). Nvidia also 'seeded' pirated books (i.e., made available and uploaded parts of a completely downloaded file). While Nvidia took some steps to limit seeding, it did not prevent seeding altogether," the complaint reads.
 
The authors say they found out in June, when Nvidia handed over the code it used for torrenting. Based on that code, they were "able to determine that Nvidia did not disable uploading," the authors told the court. The complaint states that the authors' own books were among those Nvidia downloaded. However, the claim that they were also uploaded to others is made "on information and belief," which essentially means the authors don't have direct knowledge of it. In addition to the seeding claims, the authors also allege that Nvidia shared the pirated books with business partners, including Adobe, through a "PDF Extraction Project" involving 250 million pages. These pages were acquired in part from shadow libraries such as Anna's Archive and LibGen.
 
According to the complaint, Nvidia shared its pirated books with Adobe because it wanted to "get tokens out of PDFs to create differentiated models" and "include PDF extraction into our NeMo pipeline so that customers can leverage their PDF content." In return, the complaint says, Adobe committed to using Nvidia's language models in some of its products. That made the deal a big opportunity for Nvidia, with its NeMo AI models potentially "powering every one of Adobe PDFs," the authors write. Adobe wasn't the only partner. The complaint also mentions partnerships with Cohere and Imbue that involved sharing Nvidia's base training data and offering books acquired from shadow libraries. The authors believe their own books were shared with all three companies, but this is alleged on information and belief. With these allegations, the amended complaint now accuses Nvidia of distributing the books itself and of helping others to infringe, which falls under its existing direct and contributory infringement claims.

items.title: 20 Repos, 713K Stars: The Open Source Tools That Build, Tune and Run Language Models
items.author: Text Mining
items.content:
huggingface/transformers is the most-starred repo in the whole directory, at 169.4K. This week it added 100 stars. OpenVINO, Intel's inference toolkit, has 12.8K stars and added 1.3K, thirteen times as many. That gap says where the work is now. Most teams no longer write a model from scratch. They pick one that already exists, tune it on their own data, and then fight to make it run fast and cheap on the hardware they have.

Every repo below comes from TextMining.Tech, HackerNoon's directory of 7,075 open source text mining tools, libraries and frameworks with at least 100 stars each. They're grouped by job: define the model, train or fine-tune it, then run it.

This is part 2 of a four-part series. Part 1 covered the tools that read documents, retrieve context and teach you to build. Speech and voice come next.

  • Running models is where the momentum is. The six run-and-deploy repos added about 1.9K stars this week, more than the other 14 repos combined (about 1.2K).
  • OpenVINO out-gained transformers 13 to 1. It added 1.3K stars this week against transformers' 100, from a base one-thirteenth the size.
  • A 1.2K-star newcomer is moving. halo, White Circle's training framework, added 316 stars this week, about a quarter of its total.
  • Old training repos keep their stars. stanford_alpaca (last updated July 2024) and Open-Assistant (August 2024) still hold 67.5K stars between them.
  • LlamaFactory is the fine-tuning default. At 76.3K stars, it has more than Megatron-LM, ml-engineering and halo combined (39.4K).
  • 12 of the 20 repos use Apache-2.0, 3 use MIT and 5 use another license.

Define the model: 7 repos, 313K stars

These repos hold the models themselves, or the code and data that define them. transformers is the hub most of the others plug into; the rest are model families built for a language, a domain or a different way of answering.

The model-definition framework for text, vision, audio and multimodal models, for inference and training

Non-autoregressive engine that makes typed choice, score and yes/no decisions over text in one forward pass, in 100+ languages

Microsoft's large-scale self-supervised pre-training across tasks, languages and modalities

Ready-to-use datasets for AI models, with tools to load and transform them

Alibaba Cloud's official repo for the original Qwen chat and pretrained models

Chinese LLaMA and Alpaca models, with local CPU and GPU training and deployment

laya added nearly three times as many stars as transformers this week, from a base a fifth the size.

Train and fine-tune: 7 repos, 228K stars

Once you have a base model, these repos adapt it to your data or train new ones at scale. They range from a one-stop fine-tuning toolkit to the distributed systems behind frontier-scale training, plus two 2023-era projects that taught a generation how instruction tuning works.

Unified, efficient fine-tuning for 100+ LLMs and vision-language models (ACL 2024)

Distributed compute engine with libraries for scaling training and other ML workloads

Community-built chat assistant project, including its crowd-sourced training data

Code and data generation for training Stanford's Alpaca instruction-tuned models

An open book on the engineering of training and running large models

NVIDIA's research code for training transformer models at scale

White Circle's framework for training large language and multimodal models

halo is the smallest repo in this series so far, and it added more stars this week than anything else in this group.

Run and deploy: 6 repos, 172K stars

A tuned model is only useful once it answers requests. These repos run models locally, compile them for phones and browsers, wire them into apps, and watch what they do in production.

Self-hosted engine that runs LLMs, vision, voice, image and video models on any hardware, no GPU required

AI engineering platform with a gateway, agent observability, evals and prompt management, built on OpenTelemetry

Vercel's AI SDK for building AI-powered apps and agents in TypeScript

Universal LLM deployment engine that uses ML compilation to target many devices

High-performance LLM inference that runs inside the browser

The smallest repo in this group gained the most: OpenVINO's 1.3K stars this week topped the whole Natural Language Processing category.

All numbers come from the TextMining.Tech snapshot of Nov 26, 2026. The directory tracks open source GitHub repos with at least 100 stars, excludes archived repos and forks, and refreshes daily. We started from the top repos in the Language Models and Natural Language Processing categories and kept the ones that define, train or run models. "Added this week" is the directory's own weekly star count. Stars will have moved by the time you read this, so each repo name links to its live directory page.

What's next, and where to dig further

Part 3 is speech and voice. VoiceStudio, a fully local voice cloning, dubbing and transcription suite, added 4.9K stars this week, more than all 20 repos in this list combined.

Or open the full directory of 7,075 repos, sort by "Trending this week", and see what's climbing before it makes the next list. Built something that belongs here? Once it passes 100 stars, it's in.

items.title: T5-Small Out-Downloads NLLB 24 to 1: 143 Open-Weight Translation Models Ranked
items.author: Writings, Papers and Blogs on Text Models
items.content:
Google's t5-small was downloaded 17.3M times on Hugging Face in the last 30 days. Meta's 200-language nllb-200-distilled-600M got 709.4K. Below are all 143 translation models in the TextModels directory: open weights ranked by downloads, including 73 Opus-MT language pairs from Helsinki-NLP, plus the historical models that started neural machine translation.

Downloads and capability tell different stories here. NLLB-200 covers 200 languages, and HackerNoon's look inside the AI that translates 200 languages explains how it lifted quality for low-resource languages. But t5-small is a 60M-parameter multitask model that tutorials and test suites load by default. For production in specific language pairs, teams still reach for dedicated models, as in this production voice stack for Igbo, Yoruba and Hausa that chose NLLB over an LLM.

  • Helsinki-NLP is the long tail. 73 of the 143 entries are its Opus-MT models, one per language pair.
  • English to Russian leads the pairs.opus-mt-en-ru is the most-downloaded single-pair model at 566.9K.

Everything comes from the TextModels directory as of November 23, 2026, filtered to translation models (143 entries). Hugging Face download counts are the last 30 days from the Hugging Face API. "Verified" means the directory fetched and confirmed that model's metrics. Hosted models have no public download counts, so they're listed by price or provider, and historical models link to their papers.
