    echo "MISSION STATUS: CLASSIFIED"
    echo ""
    echo "Initializing control center..."
    sleep 2
    btop
}

Save the file using , press Enter, and exit with .

Now reload your shell configuration.

Your custom welcome message appears, waits two seconds, and launches .

Of course, you'll need to have installed from the previous trick.

You can create a similar command using PowerShell functions.

First, open PowerShell and type:

If PowerShell says the profile's directory doesn't exist, create it first:

New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force `
  -Path (Split-Path $PROFILE)

Then open the profile file again. Create the file if Notepad asks.

Add the following function:

function mission {
    Clear-Host

    Write-Host "================================"
    Write-Host "     WELCOME BACK, AGENT"
    Write-Host "================================"
    Write-Host ""
    Write-Host "SYSTEM STATUS: ONLINE"
    Write-Host "MISSION STATUS: CLASSIFIED"
    Write-Host ""
    Write-Host "Initializing control center..."

    Start-Sleep -Seconds 2

    Get-Process |
        Sort-Object CPU -Descending |
        Select-Object -First 10
}

Save the file and open a new PowerShell window.

Your custom command will display the welcome message and list processes with the highest accumulated CPU time.

You don't have to stop at .

You can create commands for almost anything.

For example, on macOS or Linux, you could create a function that launches the Matrix animation:

hack() {
    clear
    cmatrix
}

Add it to your shell configuration and reload the file.

Now all you need to type is:

And your entire terminal transforms into the Matrix.

items.title: AI Could Become the Front Door to Digital Banking
items.author: Anastasiia_D
items.content:
Over the last several years, we have witnessed a real boom in AI technologies. Companies have been experimenting with agents, launching AI assistants, and trying to integrate new capabilities into existing products.

However, the initial enthusiasm is gradually colliding with reality. Building an impressive demo is much easier than launching a safe, secure, and reliable product for millions of users.

This is particularly evident in the banking sector, where companies work with sensitive financial data, face strict regulatory requirements, and where the cost of any mistake can be much higher. These challenges hinder the adoption of new technologies and bold innovations.

Over the last 10–15 years, banks have invested huge amounts of resources in developing the digital customer experience. They have introduced new functions, new services, and complex customer journeys.

Several years ago, the whole industry, not just the banking sector, was actively discussing and developing super apps — applications that bring together multiple functions, including financial and non-financial services, in one place.

Having worked on banking products, I remember how complex it was to fit so many functions into a single interface.

We conducted a lot of research. We tried to assess the clarity of the text and navigation, and we tested different screen designs. We needed to find out whether customers could find the right function or service, interpret the information correctly, and complete the entire customer journey.

The interface had to be intuitive, simple, and clear because its usability could directly affect conversion rates and other business metrics.

An entire industry has developed around UX research, design, testing, and customer behavior analysis.

But what we see today is that ChatGPT and other AI assistants, like Claude, are forming a new habit. Instead of searching for specific information or services, you can simply explain what you want to do, and the assistant helps you find the right one among a myriad of other capabilities.

And it's not just about the convenience of interacting with AI. Customers' expectations of digital products are actually changing.

A recent  found that 23% of surveyed banking consumers already use generative AI for financial tasks. Among those, 74% use ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini to ask financial questions and get help with banking-related tasks.

But a banking interface is not just a collection of screens and buttons. It reflects the underlying banking processes.

When customers navigate between screens, fill out forms, select options, and confirm operations, they are following a process designed by the bank. The interface guides them through each step.

Now imagine that customers no longer need to navigate through these steps themselves. They simply explain what they want to achieve, and an AI assistant helps them get there.

This raises an interesting question. Are we just making existing interfaces easier to use, or are we moving towards a different way of delivering services?

And this is where the difference between automation and transformation becomes important.

Today, you can find many AI assistants on the market. They help answer customers' questions, find information, and automate individual customer service processes.

But it's important to distinguish between three levels of AI adoption: assistance, automation, and transformation.

At the first level, AI helps people understand an existing process and complete tasks faster.

At the second level, AI takes over individual steps, making the whole process faster and cheaper. But we are still operating within the same process.

At the third level, we change the process itself.

Instead of asking customers to follow predefined banking processes, we start with what they actually want to achieve. AI could then determine how to deliver that outcome, combining different banking services and capabilities without requiring customers to understand how they work behind the scenes.

This is not just about making an existing process faster. It changes how customers interact with banks.

And we are already seeing early examples of this shift. In the US, eligible ChatGPT users can connect their bank accounts through  for read-only financial guidance. Banco  has taken a different approach, building an app inside ChatGPT where customers can explore its banking products without leaving the conversation.

These are still early steps rather than full process transformation. But they show something interesting:  ** **within AI platforms, allowing customers to interact with banking services without opening a traditional banking app.

What Is Holding Back the Transition?

If the potential benefits are so obvious, why are we not seeing a large-scale transition to this model?

In my opinion, one of the main challenges is, of course, security.

Recent years have demonstrated not only the capabilities of AI but also the rapid growth of security threats. In 2025 alone, AI-enabled fraud increased by 1,210% in data analyzed by .

And recent months have also brought particularly concerning examples of the difficulties in controlling autonomous AI systems.

In July 2026, during OpenAI's internal cybersecurity evaluations involving models with reduced safeguards, AI agents bypassed isolation controls and compromised parts of OpenAI's research infrastructure and . The agents took actions beyond their assigned tasks, exposing the risk of giving AI systems access to real infrastructure.

Another example came in October 2026, when researchers using AI tools helped identify and analyze critical vulnerabilities in PHP. These vulnerabilities could allow attackers to execute code remotely on vulnerable servers. This was not an AI-caused breach, but it demonstrated how AI can accelerate vulnerability research.

For banks, these risks are particularly serious. It's one thing to allow AI to answer questions about banking products, but it's something entirely different to allow it to manage financial operations or execute transactions.

Moving from an assistant that provides information to one that can take action requires a completely different level of security, control, and trust.

And not every company has the resources and expertise necessary to build its own secure infrastructure for AI agents. For smaller players, this could mean relying on specialized technology providers rather than building everything themselves.

I don't think traditional banking interfaces will disappear. I believe they will remain necessary for visualizing information, checking data, and confirming important operations.

But their role could change significantly.

So far, we have tried to make complex banking processes simple and clear for customers through interface design.

But the next step may be the opposite: making sure customers no longer need to understand the complexity of these processes.

And the real transformation will happen not when every bank launches its own AI assistant, but when AI assistants stop being just an additional feature and become a new way of interacting with banking services.

items.title: How to Investigate Suspected Bot Traffic in GA4
items.author: Shabnam Karbalaeihadi
items.content:
A spike in Direct traffic is easy to notice. The harder one to question is a spike that looks like a win. The new visitors scroll through articles, trigger plenty of events and sometimes rack up multiple page views. In a monthly performance review, that can look like audience growth.

Working in publishing SEO, I’ve learned to ask what else grew alongside those sessions. Did more readers come back? Did more people log in or subscribe? Or did most of the increase come from sessions that all looked unusually similar?

That question matters in the age of AI search, when visits from people clicking links in AI tools and requests from automated systems can both be part of the picture. A GA4 spike can tell me where to investigate. It can’t tell me which tool generated the traffic, or whether an LLM was involved.

  • Direct or Unassigned spike: find which channel, landing page and country the extra sessions came from, and rule out Discover first.
  • Unusual screen resolution: a rare square resolution like 1366 × 1366 suddenly driving most of the increase is a strong clue.
  • a high-volume segment with almost zero returning users deserves a closer look.
  • Flat logins or subscriptions: thousands of extra sessions with no change in verified account activity don’t add up to audience growth.
  • Traffic from outside your core market: geography narrows the search but is never enough to exclude traffic alone.
  • Views per session below 1: check your tagging and instrumentation before blaming automation.
  • High engagement next to other red flags: automation can scroll to 90% and stay in focus, so engagement alone doesn’t prove real readers.

No single signal proves bot traffic. I look for the same sessions matching several of them, then compare reports with and without that segment.

Signal 1. A sudden spike in Direct or Unassigned traffic

In GA4, I start in Reports → Acquisition → Traffic acquisition and compare the spike with a comparable period. I check which session default channel group changed, then break down the increase by and . I’m looking for where the sessions came from. A sitewide average can hide a surge concentrated on a single URL.

For a publisher, one of my first checks is Search Console → Discover, if the report is available. If Discover clicks climb on the same articles on the same dates, that gives me a plausible explanation for at least part of the lift, especially if referral information is missing in GA4. I compare the timing and URLs because Discover clicks and GA4 sessions are different measurements. Search Console performance reports

What I check inside the spike

Signal 2. A surge from the same unusual screen resolution

I add as a breakdown in a GA4 Exploration or check the Tech details report. I pay attention when a square resolution such as or goes from rare to accounting for a large share of the increase. The interesting part is the concentration. How common was that resolution before the spike? Does it also dominate the same landing page, browser or country? GA4 Tech details report

Signal 3. Almost no returning users in a high-volume segment

If the same cluster shows substantial volume and zero or almost zero returning users over a meaningful date range, I take a closer look. Automation can start with a fresh browser profile each time, and it can also reuse one. Real visitors can look new when GA4 can’t recognise a previous visit, and a successful acquisition campaign can bring in a genuinely new audience. I compare the suspicious group with similar traffic over the same period. GA4 user metrics

Signal 4. More sessions without more verified logins or subscriptions

On a subscription site, I check whether the extra sessions produce any verified logins or subscription activity. A SaaS team could make the same comparison with sign-ups or account activity. If a site uses a custom dimension, a wave of values tells me to check when the tag sends that value. It might be missing for genuine anonymous readers or because the implementation only sets it after login. I get more confidence from a mismatch between thousands of extra interactions and flat account activity, especially where comparable traffic normally produces some.

Signal 5. A sudden traffic surge from outside your core market

If a UK-focused publication suddenly gets a large share of its Direct sessions from Singapore or China, I check whether that lines up with distribution, coverage, or a campaign. Geography helps narrow the investigation. I’m more interested when the same sessions also share a rare resolution and repeatedly enter through one page. Country on its own is too broad a reason to exclude traffic.

Signal 6. Views per session drop below 1

below 1 is another prompt to inspect the events. GA4 counts both web page views and app screen views in this metric. If I see a low ratio, I separate web from app traffic and check whether events are arriving without their corresponding or . Missing tags or an event-only implementation can explain the same pattern. I check the instrumentation before attributing it to automation. GA4 dimensions and metrics

Signal 7. Strong engagement alongside other red flags

GA4 records engagement time while a page is in focus or an app is in the foreground. An engaged session can qualify by passing the engagement-time threshold, recording a key event, or reaching two page or screen views. The default enhanced-measurement scroll event fires when 90% of the page becomes visible. Browser automation can navigate to a second page, keep a page in focus and scroll deep enough to trigger the same event. These metrics describe what the browser reported. They can look healthy even when I still have questions about who generated the activity. GA4 user engagement · Sessions · Automatically collected events

I also check unusually long engagement against the metric’s denominator. More than a day of engagement across a large group can be ordinary. More than a day of average engagement per session is a reason to inspect event timestamps and tracking. The GA4 default of 30 minutes, adjustable up to 7 hours and 55 minutes, is an . It measures how long a session can sit idle before expiring, so it doesn’t set a hard ceiling on the length of an active session. GA4 session timeout

Google Analytics already excludes traffic from known bots and spiders automatically. For traffic that still looks suspicious, I build a session segment around the combination I’ve observed, such as an unusual resolution and a specific landing page within the channel that spiked. I compare with traffic excluding that segment across sessions, engagement and meaningful outcomes. If a rule also captures traffic I can tie to a genuine Discover spike or verified subscribers, I narrow it. GA4 known bot exclusion

Here’s how I set that up in a GA4 Exploration:

  1. Go to and start a exploration.
  2. Next to , click and choose .
  3. Add conditions that match the pattern, for example exactly matches and matches the URL that spiked. Name it .
  4. Create a second segment for the channel that spiked and use with the same conditions. This gives you the adjusted view.
  5. Apply both segments and compare sessions, returning users, engagement and key events side by side.

Where I have access, I ask the web team to compare the same URLs and time windows against CDN or server logs. Repeated request sequences or an existing bot classification can strengthen the case. Until I have that corroboration, I label the segment . I keep the original totals visible alongside the adjusted view so stakeholders can see how much the rule changes the story.

In an illustrative example, Direct sessions fell from to once the segment was excluded, while all verified logins and subscriptions remained in the adjusted view. The outcomes didn’t move, which told me the extra sessions weren’t new readers.

Set up a custom insight to catch the next bot traffic spike

Once you know which patterns deserve attention, you can use GA4 custom insights to get an email when traffic changes unexpectedly. An alert gives you a reason to investigate using the signals above.

  1. You need the role on the property to create, edit and share custom insights. Ask your GA4 administrator to confirm your permissions or create the insight for you.
  2. Open the Insights dashboard. Select your property, go to and scroll to the section. Click , then .
  3. Under , click . You can also select beside a suggested insight and adapt its conditions.
  4. Choose the evaluation frequency. Select Hourly, Daily, Weekly or Monthly. Hourly evaluation is available for web data only. Daily is a practical starting point for monitoring changes alongside your regular reporting.
  5. Define the segment and trigger. Under , click to narrow the traffic using the dimensions available, for example Direct traffic. Choose an available metric and condition. lets GA4 identify an unusual change without a numerical threshold. Alternatively, choose a percentage-increase condition and set a threshold, such as , after checking the comparison period shown in the setup. Treat that threshold as a starting example and adjust it to your site's normal variability.
  6. Give the insight a clear name. Include the brand, frequency and reason for the alert. For example, “Brand name | Daily Direct traffic spike | Possible automation” helps colleagues recognise which property and pattern need attention.
  7. Configure email notifications and save. In the notification settings, enter the email addresses of property users who should receive the alert. Click . Triggered insights also appear in the property's Insights dashboard.
  8. Set up alerts for each property you monitor. Custom insights belong to individual properties, so check the configuration in each one. GA4 supports up to 50 custom insights per property.

When an alert arrives, compare the spike with campaigns and Discover performance, then examine screen resolution, returning users, geography and account outcomes. The same alert could also flag a successful article or a tracking issue. Google's guide to Analytics Insights

In a publishing report, I’d rather explain why sessions rose while verified subscriptions and returning readership stayed flat than turn that spike into an audience-growth claim. The question I bring back to the dashboard is simple.

If we take out the sessions that all behave the same way, would we still make the same decision?

Does GA4 filter bot traffic automatically?

Yes, for known bots. Google Analytics automatically excludes traffic from known bots and spiders, and you can’t turn this off or see how much was excluded. Automation that isn’t on a known list can still reach your reports, which is why the signals above are worth checking.

Can I create a custom bot filter in GA4?

Not directly. GA4’s built-in data filters are designed for internal and developer traffic, so there is no dedicated filter for suspected bots. Instead, I build a segment around the pattern I’ve observed and compare reports with and without it.

Can I remove bot traffic from GA4 data retroactively?

No. Data that GA4 has already processed stays in the property, and data filters only apply going forward. For past periods, I use segments or comparisons in Explorations to show the adjusted view next to the original totals.

Is every spike in Direct traffic caused by bots?

No. Google Discover, untagged email or app links, redirects that drop the referrer and links shared in private messages can all show up as Direct or Unassigned. I check those explanations before labelling any traffic as suspected automation.

Can GA4 tell me whether traffic came from an AI agent or an LLM?

Not reliably. GA4 can show referrals from AI tools when the referrer is passed, but it can’t tell you which tool generated automated visits. A spike shows you where to investigate. Server or CDN logs give you stronger evidence.

items.title: Off-Grid Messaging with MeshCore: How to Text When the Cell Towers Go Dark
items.author: Bruce Li
items.content:
A beginner's guide to MeshCore LoRa mesh radios: how they work, which hardware to buy, and how to fix the classic problem where you can hear the mesh but it can't hear you.

I have a weakness for radios that nobody needs permission to use. In a previous life, I braved 5°F winter days scanning public Wi-Fi all over downtown Helsinki, warmed by nothing but spiked glögg. Wi-Fi taught me that a little unlicensed spectrum and a lot of clever engineering can change the world. Ham radio taught me that the best communications gear is the kind that still works when everything else has given up. So when I found a $40 radio that could text people miles away, with no towers, no SIM card and no license, I had a new hobby before I'd finished reading the product page.

It also exposed a blind spot in my emergency kit. Water: check. Forty pounds of freeze-dried lasagna: check. Hand-crank flashlight that doubles as a phone charger: check. And under , a phone. A phone that is, in practice, a very expensive flashlight once the nearest cell tower loses power.

Off-grid mesh networking fills that gap: cheap long-range radios that form their own text network, with no carrier in sight. I spent the past couple of months on the Bay Area's MeshCore network with a handful of radios, one SDR dongle, and more patience than I knew I had. For ten frustrating days I could hear the whole mesh, and it couldn't hear me. This guide covers what I wish I'd known on day one: why people do this, how MeshCore works, what to buy, and how to fix the problem almost every beginner hits.

1. Why Are People Doing This?

Because the grid has a habit of blinking

Modern communication is a long chain of things that need electricity and a business model: towers, backhaul fiber, data centers, and the goodwill of your carrier. Break any link and your $1,200 slab of glass is reduced to playing the offline games you never installed.

After Hurricane Helene in September 2024, parts of western North Carolina lost power and cell service for days, in places for weeks. In April 2025, the Iberian blackout took mobile service down across Spain and Portugal within hours, once tower backup batteries ran dry.

In the Bay Area, I don't have to imagine it. We have earthquake faults under our feet and fire seasons that bring planned PG&E power shutoffs. On October 27, 2019, high winds, a forest fire and a PG&E shutoff took out my power, internet and cable TV all at once. The Mercury News wrote about it, and I ended up building a cardboard-and-tinfoil antenna to watch Sunday football over the air.

Mesh radios don't care. They run for days on a small battery, indefinitely on a palm-sized solar panel, and relay messages through each other instead of through a tower.

The non-apocalyptic reasons

  • hikers and sailors beyond the last bar of signal, and festivals where 50,000 people crush the cell network.
  • neighborhoods putting solar repeaters on rooftops as a permanent backup network.
  • a network you own, with no carrier logging your metadata.
  • honestly the big one, and my reason. It's ham radio for people who'd rather flash firmware than memorize Morse code, and you don't need a license.

2. LoRa and Mesh: A Short Primer

LoRa: long range, low everything else

First, a naming hazard. (lowercase , "Long Range") is a radio modulation owned by Semtech. It has nothing to do with , the AI fine-tuning trick. I spend a lot of time around AI people, and I can confirm that search engines find this hilarious.

LoRa uses : each symbol is a tone sweeping across a slice of spectrum. Because the receiver knows the shape of the chirp, it can dig a signal out from the noise floor. That's how a radio putting out about as much power as a phone's Wi-Fi reaches miles instead of yards.

The trade-off is bandwidth: a few hundred bits to a few kilobits per second. Enough for a text or a GPS position, never enough for a photo of your dog. LoRa runs in unlicensed ISM bands: 915 MHz in the Americas and Australia/New Zealand, 868 MHz in Europe and the UK. Sub-gigahertz signals pass through trees, walls and San Francisco fog far better than Wi-Fi. Karl the Fog is not the problem. The hills are.

Mesh: everyone is the tower

A cell network is a : lose the tower and everyone in range goes silent. A has no center. Radios pass messages along, hop by hop, until they arrive.

Where it fits among the radios you know

Cellular and Wi-Fi depend on someone else's infrastructure. Ham radio doesn't, but it takes an exam, real skill, and (in most countries) a ban on encryption. LoRa mesh is what I'd hand to my non-radio-nerd family: no license, encrypted, days on a battery, and it looks like a messaging app.

3. Meshtastic vs. MeshCore, and Why I Chose MeshCore

Both big projects run on the same cheap LoRa boards. They're different with opposite ideas about who should relay.

  • is the big, friendly one, with the largest community and the most polished apps. Every radio relays every message, up to 7 hops. Two radios out of the box just work. The catch: in a dense city, hundreds of pocket radios rebroadcasting everything eat the airtime.
  • is the younger, more opinionated challenger. Your pocket radio never relays. Fixed repeaters on rooftops and hills do all of it, and after the first message, traffic follows a learned route instead of flooding. It scales to whole regions. The catch: somebody has to climb onto a roof. (Two MeshCore radios in range of each other can still talk directly.)

Not built in (on purpose)

Groups on the move, first-timers

City- and region-wide networks

The honest verdict: for a group that moves around together and wants something that works out of the box, pick Meshtastic. If your city has MeshCore repeaters, or you want to help build permanent regional coverage, pick MeshCore.

Around the Bay, the second case is winning.

That's what a mesh looks like when it delivers reliably enough for real conversation. The Bay Area MeshCore crowd has put hundreds of repeaters on rooftops, hilltops and the occasional tree. One of my test messages was heard by 66 of them, across a span of 238 miles. The two networks can't talk to each other, so the right choice is whichever one your neighbors run. Mine run MeshCore.

4. How MeshCore Works: The Journey of a Message

MeshCore's design fits on a napkin. There are three kinds of node:

  • are personal radios: a handheld with a keyboard, or a little board paired to the MeshCore phone app. They anyone else's traffic.
  • are fixed, usually solar-powered, and do all the relaying.
  • are bulletin boards that hold messages for people who were offline.

Every node has a cryptographic key pair, and the public key its identity: no accounts, servers or phone numbers. Nodes introduce themselves with an , a signed packet carrying their public key, a name, and optionally a location. Repeaters advert every 12 hours. Companions advert only when you tell them to, so press that button when you're new, or nobody will know you exist.

Every message is one small packet

A packet gets repeated by anyone who hasn't already; a one only by the next repeater on its path. Repeaters forward your words but can't read them.

Alice in Berkeley texts Bob in San Jose. Both have advertised, so each has the other's public key.

  1. Alice's radio combines her private key and Bob's public key into a secret only the two of them share, encrypts the text with AES-128, adds a short authentication tag, and sends it as a flood with an empty path.
  2. Repeaters relay once and sign the guest book. Each repeater that hears the packet checks whether it has seen it before. If not, it waits a short random moment (longer if the signal was weak, so strong links win the race), appends its own ID to the path, and re-sends. The ripple dies out on its own, because nobody repeats a packet twice.
  3. Bob answers with the map. Bob's radio decrypts the message and sends back a : the list of repeaters the message took, with the delivery receipt tucked inside. Alice's screen shows "delivered," and her radio saves the route.
  4. Alice's next message carries that route in its header. Repeaters not on the list stay silent, even if they heard every byte. One message now costs a handful of transmissions instead of a regional flood.

If the route breaks (say, a repeater loses power), Alice's radio retries three times and floods the last attempt to find a new route.

Group channels always flood, because "everyone in #test" has no single destination. A channel is just a shared key. uses a well-known key, and a channel's key is derived from its name, so anyone who guesses the name can read along. Treat both as billboards.

Two honest caveats. The cryptography is lean (tiny authentication tags, no forward secrecy): fine for a camping trip, not for a nation-state threat model. And with only 256 possible 1-byte repeater IDs, busy regions get collisions, which is why the Bay Area mesh is moving to 2-byte IDs.

5. Choosing Hardware and Software for MeshCore

Lessons from my own drawer of radios

Check official support before you buy. My first rig was an M5Stack Cardputer ADV, a credit-card-sized computer with a keyboard, plus the snap-on Cap LoRa-1262 radio with GPS. Meshtastic supports it officially. MeshCore didn't, so I ended up writing my own MeshCore firmware for it (it's on M5Burner as , if you have one). Fun hobby, not a beginner's path. Before buying anything, find your board in the MeshCore web flasher. If it isn't listed, you're on your own.

Decide how you want to type. are small boards paired to the MeshCore phone app: cheap, simple, and the app is good. But your phone becomes part of the system, and in a real outage you'll want its battery for other things. have their own screen and keyboard and need no phone at all. That's what I'd want in a go-bag.

Battery life depends on the chip. Radios built on Nordic's chips sip power, often running a week or more on a small battery. radios are more capable but hungrier: with the screen off, my Cardputer draws 120–150 mA, so its 1,500 mAh battery lasts 10–12 hours, not days. For something that sits in a bag listening, nRF52 wins.

GPS costs more than battery life. On my radio, the running GPS receiver raised the LoRa noise floor by about 4 dB, making it measurably deafer. Keep GPS off unless you actually need your position.

Newest isn't always best. I tested a brand-new radio built on Semtech's fourth-generation LR2021 chip (most radios use the second-generation SX1262). On a cheap SDR dongle it showed two problems: it sent the start of each packet about 25 dB too quietly, and it sat 23 kHz off frequency. The first turned out to be a firmware bug, which I've since patched in my own build. The second happens because the board has no (a temperature-compensated crystal), which matters on MeshCore's narrow 62.5 kHz channels. Prefer boards with a TCXO, and let other people beta-test the shiny new silicon.

Get an external antenna connector. You'll want to upgrade the antenna (see section 7), so look for SMA or RP-SMA, not a tiny internal antenna.

It sounds greedy, but a second, known-good radio is the best diagnostic tool you'll ever own. It's how I proved my problem wasn't my hardware.

If I were starting over, I'd get a with the community-built WadaMesh firmware, which is much nicer to use than the official T-Deck build. It looks like a BlackBerry that took up survivalism: thumb keyboard, trackball, 2.8-inch touchscreen, GPS, a 2,000 mAh battery and an SX1262 radio with a TCXO. No phone required. It was also my known-good reference through every test in this article.

Buy the right for your region: 915 MHz for the Americas and ANZ, 868 MHz for Europe and the UK. Buying the wrong one is the hobby's most common rite of passage.

For everything else, start from the Bay Area MeshCore recommended devices list. It's written by the people who run the repeaters and is refreshingly honest about weak spots. Condensed, with my pick on top:

Keyboard, screen, GPS, battery; no phone needed.

ESP32, so shorter battery life.

Best-value starter: screen, GPS, battery, external antenna. About 5 days per charge. Ships with MeshCore.

3D-printed case, not waterproof. Upgrade the antenna.

Meshnology N39 (Heltec V4 kit)

Complete kit with case, GPS and OLED. Strong transmit power, which helps you get heard.

ESP32, so shorter battery life. Not waterproof.

The classic: e-ink screen, great battery life, lots of community know-how.

Weak stock antenna, small battery, fragile buttons.

Credit-card size, IP65 sealed.

Sealed antenna hears well but struggles to be heard.

Seeed SenseCAP Solar Node P1-Pro

5 W solar panel, big battery, reportedly two weeks without sun.

Swap the 2 dBi stock antenna. Not IP-rated.

RAK WisMesh Repeater Mini

Most weatherproof: IP67 throughout.

Smaller panel and battery. RP-SMA connector.

Prices from the Bay Area MeshCore list, last updated March 2026. Most of these ship with Meshtastic; flash MeshCore once when it arrives.

Notice the pattern: almost every entry says "upgrade the antenna." It's usually the single biggest improvement you can make, and the first fix for the lopsided-link problem in section 7. Check that the connector (SMA, RP-SMA or N-type) matches your device, or order an adapter too.

never power on a LoRa radio without an antenna attached. Transmitting into nothing can fry the radio chip, a lesson almost everyone learns once.

MeshCore lives or dies by repeaters, so check there's a network before you spend a cent.

  • The official MeshCore map shows repeaters and room servers near you.
  • Find your local group and use . If your preset doesn't match your neighbors', you won't hear a thing. Mine is Bay Area MeshCore: device recommendations, setup guides, a channel list, live maps, a network health check, and a Discord full of people suspiciously happy to answer beginner questions. Most metro areas have one; search for "[your city] MeshCore".
  • No repeaters nearby? Then you're putting up the first one, or Meshtastic may suit your area better for now.

Step 1: Flash and say hello

A few radios, like the Wio Tracker L1 Pro, arrive with MeshCore installed; most ship with Meshtastic. Either way, flash the latest release. No soldering and no compiler, just a USB cable and Chrome. Open flasher.meshcore.io, pick your board, and pick a : for your pocket radio, for the roof. Bluetooth companions then pair with the MeshCore phone app.

Set your (this is the legal part, so don't skip it), press so others can find you, and send your first message. Mine was "Hi" on Public. Nobody replied to this clueless newbie. As it turned out, nobody had heard him.

Step 2: Be a good neighbor

  • Ask before you add a repeater. A badly configured one adds flood traffic for everybody. Local groups have conventions for names, advert intervals and IDs.
  • Test on #test, and don't advert on a timer.
  • Use your region's preset and respect its power limits. In the US, once your antenna gain passes 6 dBi, the allowed transmit power goes , not up.
  • The best thing you can do for a MeshCore network is put a solar repeater somewhere high. The second best is answering a beginner's question.

7. "I Can Hear Them, but They Can't Hear Me"

This is the most common beginner problem in MeshCore. It cost me ten days.

Your radio fills up with repeaters and messages. But anything you send disappears: channel messages never come back as repeats, DMs never show as delivered, and nobody replies. It feels like a broken transmitter. It almost never is.

Radio paths work the same in both directions, but the two ends of the link don't:

  • Repeaters shout, you whisper. Some repeaters run 1-watt amplifiers and big antennas on hilltops. Your handheld puts out about a sixth of that through a stubby antenna at waist height.
  • Repeaters live in a noisy neighborhood. A hilltop hears every gadget, smart meter and radio in the valley. Its noise floor is higher than your quiet room's, so your weak signal has more to cut through.
  • Listening is easy, being heard is hard. You only need to hear of the dozens of repeaters around you to see traffic. To get a message out, at least one of them has to hear .
  • In Meshtastic, a nearby handheld might relay for you. In MeshCore, it's a repeater or nothing.

The upshot: being 4–6 dB short of the nearest repeater is enough to lose most of your sends. That's less than the difference between your desk and your window.

How I proved it wasn't my radio

Like any engineer, I blamed my gear and spent a week swapping settings, firmware and suspicions about every component on the board. Two things finally cracked it.

First, a . I bought a T-Deck Plus, and it failed from my house too. Then I used a as a crude power meter, with both radios taking turns on the same marked spot. My Cardputer was never weaker than the T-Deck.

Second, . From a hillside, the same radio heard about 30 repeaters instead of one. Every message got through, and it scored 84–87% on the Bay Area health check, which counts how many of the region's listening stations hear your message. The T-Deck scored 82% from the same spot.

Same radio, same firmware, same antenna. The bug was my house.

  1. Most MeshCore apps can run a , which asks nearby repeaters to reply, and some show the signal both ways. If repeaters hear you at −10 dB SNR while you hear them at +3 dB, you've found your imbalance. Use your region's health check if it has one.
  2. Test several times from one spot. Conditions swing from minute to minute. I once had the identical setup succeed on one run and fail completely on the next. One send tells you nothing. Five tell you something.
  3. Stock antennas are decorative. My $12–15 Muzi Works 915 MHz whip took me from hearing nothing indoors to seeing a repeater within minutes.
  4. A windowsill beats a desk, upstairs beats downstairs, and a balcony beats both. Point at the hills where the repeaters live, and get the antenna outside if you can: walls and low-E coated windows eat several dB.
  5. Upgrade to a higher-power radio. One-watt LoRa radios don't cost much more. RAK's WisMesh 1W Booster Starter Kit is sold for Meshtastic but runs MeshCore once you flash it. A big amplifier plus a big antenna can quickly take you past the legal limit, though. In the US, FCC Part 15.247 allows 1 W into the antenna, and above 6 dBi of antenna gain you must turn the power down dB for dB: 36 dBm EIRP in total.
  6. Put a node where the signal is. If your home is a dead zone, put a second radio with a better antenna on the balcony or roof, and pair to it over Bluetooth from indoors. Or, with your local group's blessing, put up a repeater. It's the most useful thing you can do for everyone.

One company makes the magic chirp. Nearly every LoRa radio runs Semtech silicon or a licensed copy. That's a supply risk, not a kill switch: the firmware is open source, and nobody can switch your radio off remotely. A movement against centralized infrastructure that depends on one chip supplier. Irony noted.

License-free isn't rule-free. ISM bands have power limits, and unlicensed users get no protection from interference. Your "I'm okay" has no more right to the airwaves than your neighbor's weather station.

Encrypted doesn't mean invisible. Public and #hashtag channels are readable by anyone, and adverts can carry your location. Leave location sharing off, especially if your bug-out cabin is a secret.

Repeaters are volunteers. Coverage depends on other people's rooftops and batteries. Treat the mesh as one layer of your comms plan: two is one, and one is none.

  • A 1-watt booster or a repeater. A RAK booster board with a directional patch antenna, so I can hear well and be heard. And if I get a repeater up, I can help our local coverage too.
  • A proper side-by-side of the two meshes, on the same hills.

The dark horse: Reticulum

Reticulum isn't a mesh app but a whole cryptographic network stack that runs over LoRa, Wi-Fi, packet radio, the internet, or anything else that moves bytes. It takes config files and patience, and around the Bay I could barely find anyone on it. And no, it can't bridge MeshCore and Meshtastic; today that takes a gateway, a Raspberry Pi with one radio from each tribe.

  • Bigger IDs, fewer collisions. MeshCore's move to 2- and 3-byte repeater IDs will make busy regional meshes easier to trace and debug.
  • Every new keyboard radio with official MeshCore support removes the "now install this phone app" step for non-technical users.

MeshCore won't replace your phone. It's slow, text-only, and it works only because a few hundred neighbors put radios on their roofs. But that's rather the point: it's a network built by the people who use it, out of cheap radios and spare rooftops, and it keeps working when the expensive one doesn't. And when you can't get through, the answer is almost never in your settings. It's in the sky: go higher, see farther, and join the people already up there.

My T-Deck now lives in my go-bag, next to the lasagna. For the price of a takeout dinner, you can put one in yours that will, on the worst day of the year, still get the message through:

"We're fine. Bring water. And the lasagna."

  • Bay Area traffic chart: data from a Bay Area MeshCore member who runs nodes on both networks
  • Cardputer and T-Deck Plus photos, SDR and health-check measurements: the author
  • Diagrams (chirp spectrogram, star vs. mesh, range vs. speed, packet anatomy, message journey, flood vs. direct, line of sight): original illustrations made for this article

items.title: James T. Russell, Physicist Who Pioneered CD and DVD Technology, Dies At 95
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
James T. Russell, the American physicist whose pioneering digital-to-optical recording and playback system laid the foundation for CD, DVD and Blu-ray technology, has died at the age of 95. "Russell never became a household name, but the technology he developed, later licensed by Sony and Phillips, would transform everything from the way people listen to music to the way data is stored," reports The Daily Chronicle. From the report: In a career spanning almost his entire life, Russell earned more than 70 patents, but his biggest breakthrough was the invention of the first digital-to-optical recording and playback system in the 1960s and early 1970s, a system that brought crystal clear audio and film to the masses. [...] It was in Richland that Russell started exploring how to create cleaner recordings of music. Popping and hissing often accompanied the music of vinyl records, from the analog sound of a needle scraping against microgrooves, and Russell thought he could do something about it. He crunched the numbers before bringing an invention report to Battelle: What if a light beam could read a digital record?
 
"It isn't clear what the problem was," Russell recalled in a Seattle Times interview in 2004. "I think there was some feeling amongst the moneybags that it probably wouldn't work, (or) if it did work there's no advantage, no value in optical records. What would you use it for, and would people want it and, anyway, if it was any good, IBM would have already invented it." While his idea faced skepticism early on, the company gave him some money to experiment. Russell invented an early method to store audio digitally and play it back to produce a flawless sound. He also created a way to store digital information densely.
 
Other primitive, analog laser disk technology had been developed in the 1950s by engineer David Paul Gregg. Russell's earliest patents in the field were issued in the mid-1960s, with a working prototype finished by the 1970s, using a laser to read binary data on a compact disc, or CD. The patent for Russell's invention passed from company to company, bringing him from Richland to Salt Lake City, then to Toronto. His development of the first digital-to-optical recording and playback system became foundational to CD-ROM, DVD and Blu-ray technology. Russell didn't earn royalties, never made a fortune, and was rarely credited for his work.

items.title: Why Topscan.me Stopped Counting Vulnerabilities and Started Scoring Its SLA
items.author: Nica Furs
items.content:
The Security Score on Topscan.me's dashboard used to move the wrong way when a team looked harder. Switch a workspace from monthly scans to weekly, or finally point the scanner at the staging box nobody had touched in two years, and the number at the top of the screen would fall. Security had not changed that morning. Only the visible part of the estate had grown, and the model read visibility as damage.

The company rebuilt the model earlier this year. The technical detail here comes from Topscan's Chief Product Officer, Aleksandr Melnichuk.

How the First Security Score Worked

The original Security Score was a deduction model in the plainest sense. Start at 100. Subtract a weight for every open finding, scaled by severity. Subtract more for anything already past its remediation deadline. Cap the total so a large backlog could not drive the figure to zero, and display the result as a 0-100 health number that a CTO could put in front of a board.

The logic is hard to argue with in the abstract. Fewer open vulnerabilities is better than more, and critical ones should weigh more than low ones.

Once it ran on real workspaces, the score turned out to move when nothing had changed. Import a set of AWS assets, or run a discovery pass that surfaces subdomains from a campaign site nobody remembers owning, and the score drops the same day. Those vulnerabilities were there the whole time. Finding them is progress, and the model logged it as decline.

Worse, it rewarded not looking, and this is the part that decided the rewrite. If open findings cost points, the cheapest way to hold a good score is to scan less often and leave the awkward hosts off the target list. Nobody sits down and plans that. The incentive is there anyway.

And it could not tell whether anyone was keeping their promises. A workspace with 200 findings, every one of them inside its remediation window and moving, was charged for all 200. A workspace with a dozen findings that had been ignored for six weeks was charged for twelve, plus the overdue surcharge, so the team doing the work was charged for far more findings than the team with the shorter list.

"A score that drops when you scan more is not measuring security. It is measuring how much you have admitted to," says Melnichuk. "We had shipped a score that paid people to look away. Once you notice that, you cannot really leave it alone."

A Security Score Built on SLA Deadlines

One rule carries the whole model: a finding resolved inside its deadline costs nothing at all, not even a small deduction.

The score only starts to drop when a finding passes the deadline attached to its severity, and from that day the penalty grows for as long as the finding stays open. Severity sets how heavy the penalty is, so a critical past its date costs considerably more than a low. Once a rescan no longer detects the finding, Topscan marks it fixed, the penalty stops and the score climbs back.

The deadlines are the defaults listed on the Topscan.me vulnerability management page: critical in 7 days, high in 30, medium in 60, low in 90. The timer starts at first detection, not at the most recent scan and not at the moment somebody created a ticket. A finding still detected in later scans keeps its original deadline.

Topscan does not publish the exact point weights, and old ones printed here would mostly hand you a number to misquote later. The shape is the part worth arguing about, and Topscan's help center spells it out together with its exceptions, so anyone reading the score can check what moved it.

Two Workspaces under Both Models

Consider a workspace with 140 open findings across a wide estate. The oldest was first seen nine days ago and carries a 30-day window. Nothing is past its date. That workspace scores 100.

A second workspace has eleven open findings, three of them critical and first detected five weeks ago. It loses points, and keeps losing more until someone fixes or snoozes those criticals.

The old model took the count as the headline fact and charged the first team for all 140 of them, which is close to the opposite of what the number was supposed to say. The new one says something narrower and more useful: the first team has nothing past its deadline, and the second has criticals that are weeks overdue.

The scanning incentive flips along with it. Detection is free now. Pointing the scanner at a forgotten host costs zero points on the day you find whatever is running on it, and hands you a full remediation window to deal with it.

The Escape Hatch Took the Longest

Goodhart's law is the standard warning here: when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. In vulnerability management**,** it takes a very specific shape. If the metric punishes overdue work, and a team has a finding they genuinely cannot fix this month because the vendor has not shipped a patch or the deployment window is two weeks out, then the metric is quietly pushing them to close the ticket and move on.

So the model needs a legitimate way to say "not now", or it will get an illegitimate one.

Snoozing an issue pauses its SLA countdown for a chosen period. While it is paused, the finding does not count as overdue and does not penalize the score, but it stays tracked, and when the snooze expires, the timer resumes from where it stopped instead of starting over. A snooze that resets the clock would hand the finding a fresh full deadline every time someone pressed it.

The model also declines to charge teams for things that are not their work. Informational findings with no CVE attached are classed as noise and never counted. A finding marked as a false positive drops out of scoring and out of SLA tracking entirely, though if a later scan sees it again it returns to the current list, on the theory that something on the target may have changed since the last time a human judged it.

"Every metric a team is measured on has a cheat code, and the design question is which one you hand them," Melnichuk says. "I would much rather someone press snooze with a date on it than close a ticket that is not fixed. One of those keeps the finding on the board."

What the Score Still Leaves Out

Melnichuk's list of what the score misses starts with coverage, which the score says nothing about. A workspace scanning three assets out of forty can hold a perfect 100 while being blind to most of its own perimeter. Topscan chose not to patch that hole from inside the score, on the grounds that folding coverage into the same figure would have made both halves unreadable. Scan coverage sits next to the score as its own number: targets scanned in the last 30 days against total targets.

"You can get a hundred by scanning three things and fixing them on time. That is the obvious hole in it," Melnichuk says. "We left it visible instead of hiding it in the formula. A single figure that quietly folds in everything stops being checkable, and a number nobody can check does not survive contact with an auditor."

Severity still comes from CVSS. A CVSS base score describes how bad a flaw would be if exploited, and on its own it says nothing about whether anyone is exploiting it on infrastructure like yours. The product surfaces a separate exploit-known flag for findings with a working public exploit, and in day-to-day triage that flag deserves more weight than a CVSS band does. The wider industry is moving the same way. CISA's BOD 26-04, issued in June 2026, revoked the older directive that tied federal civilian agencies' patch deadlines to CVSS severity and replaced it with a decision table built from four facts about each finding: whether the asset is publicly exposed, whether the CVE is in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, how automatable the attack is, and how much control a successful attack hands over. EPSS, which estimates the probability that a CVE will be exploited in the next 30 days, pushes the same way. Topscan's score has not caught up with that yet: it weighs severity and lateness, and exploit-known findings are flagged separately.

The deadlines are a policy, too. The 7 / 30 / 60 / 90 ladder is a common vendor default, not a requirement of any major framework. Wherever a team gets to set its own numbers, a score built on deadlines inherits them, and a longer window makes the same backlog look healthier. That is survivable as long as the policy is visible to whoever reads the score, which is also why the cumulative SLA compliance rate is reported separately. It covers the whole history of a workspace, and a good week can lift it but cannot erase past late fixes, so it is the figure to bring to an audit conversation, while the score reflects what is overdue right now.

Lessons for Anyone Designing a Vulnerability Management Metric

Two decisions in this story go further than the arithmetic.

The first is choosing what the metric charges for, because that is what its users will optimize whether or not anyone meant them to. Topscan's charges for missed promises. Discovery is free, and so is a backlog that grew because somebody finally looked. By Melnichuk's account that single choice changed more behavior than any weighting adjustment did.

The second is designing the exception before shipping, before somebody games the metric. A deferral path bolted on later tends to arrive as a workaround with a feature name. The pause exists because a real team, on a real Tuesday, will have a finding they cannot fix yet and a number they are being judged on.

The count did not disappear, incidentally. Open criticals and highs still sit on the dashboard, one panel over, where they tell you what to open first. They no longer set the headline number.

The current model is described in Topscan's help center. Quotes and the account of the earlier model come from an interview with Aleksandr Melnichuk, Chief Product Officer at Topscan.me.

items.title: Scientists Used Seabirds To Track Hidden Ships
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Scientists equipped seabirds with audio recorders and GPS trackers to detect fishing vessels that were not broadcasting their locations through the Automatic Identification System (AIS), according to a new study published in Science Advances. They found that unseen vessels accounted for about 32% of vessel-related audio detections in the North Atlantic and 12% in the Mediterranean. "The one petrel in the study interacted with vessels in the South Pacific, but its geolocation device was damaged, so it was not possible to calculate how many ships it encountered had their trackers off," adds 404 Media. From the report: Many vessels are required to continuously signal their location using the Automatic Identification System (AIS), which openly broadcasts a ship's location, similar to flight tracking. But AIS can be disabled for legitimate reasons -- such as evading pirates -- or with more nefarious motivations, such as concealment of illegal fishing activities. The new study was not designed to interrogate why any particular vessel switched off its AIS tracker. However, the discovery that seabirds are regularly interacting with unseen ships can shed light on broader efforts to monitor commercial fisheries, while also revealing new insights about seabird behavior, especially their risk of becoming "bycatch" when they are fatally trapped in fishing gear.
 
Unseen vessel activity "is concerning, or at least important, regardless of whether it's legal or illegal," said Jonathan Rutter, a postdoctoral research fellow at the University of Oxford who led the study, in a call with 404 Media. He added that the recordings were not intended to be used for law-enforcement or surveillance, but that this line of research could become a "powerful tool for improving risk assessment" by recording seabird-vessel interactions that would otherwise be off the map.

items.title: We Swapped Our MCP Server's Base Image and Went From 36 Reported Vulnerabilities to Zero
items.author: Abhimanyu Garg
items.content:
We run a small internal tool a custom MCP server, the kind of thing more teams are now standing up to give AI agents access to internal systems like GitHub or Slack. It runs as a container, same as everything else. We hadn’t scrutinized its base image the way we would a customer-facing service, mostly because it never occurred to us that it needed the same level of attention. So we migrated it from a standard base image to a hardened one and measured what actually changed, rather than assuming the usual advice about “minimal images” applied here the way it does everywhere else.

Both builds used the same application source and declared dependencies (, ); the runtime base changed from Debian-based Node () to Alpine-based Docker Hardened Images (dhi.io/node:24-alpine3.23), built via a multi-stage Dockerfile with a variant for the build stage. Both images were scanned with Docker Scout on September 28, 2026, on the same architecture (). Because the distribution changed along with the image provider, treat the numbers below as a comparison of these two specific builds, not an isolated measurement of what hardening alone contributes some of the difference reflects Alpine’s smaller footprint relative to Debian, independent of the hardening effort itself.

This is a single migration of a single tool, not a controlled study across image types treat it as one documented data point, not a general verdict on any vendor's product.

Everything needed to reproduce this is public in the hardened-mcp-server repository: the MCP server source, both Dockerfiles, and the GitHub Actions workflow that builds, smoke-tests and scans each image. The numbers below come from one CI run on September 28, 2026.

Image size (Docker Scout)

Vulnerabilities reported by Docker Scout, Sept 28, 2026

36 (0 Critical / 6 High / 6 Medium / 24 Low)

Zero vulnerabilities reported by Docker Scout on this date – not “provably free of vulnerabilities”. A scan is a snapshot against a known-CVE database at a point in time, not a guarantee about what hasn’t been disclosed yet.

Note: Docker Scout’s size report for the standard image is 104 MB but plain lists it as 255 MB. For the hardened image, Docker Scout lists it as 56 MB but plain lists it as 135 MB. The gap is expected: shows the uncompressed size on local disk, while Docker Scout reports the compressed size.

The hardened build is a two-stage Dockerfile. The tag includes a shell and npm, so dependencies are installed there. The runtime stage uses the plain tag, which has no shell, and only receives the files the server needs to run.

# Build stage: -dev tag has a shell and toolchain
FROM dhi.io/node:24-alpine3.23-dev AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY src/ ./src/

# Runtime stage: no shell, only the built artifacts
FROM dhi.io/node:24-alpine3.23
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build --chown=node:node /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=build --chown=node:node /app/src ./src
COPY --from=build --chown=node:node /app/package.json ./package.json

ENV PORT=3000
EXPOSE 3000
USER node
CMD ["node", "src/server.js"]

Pulling from needs a free Docker ID and a one-time . DHI tags change on Docker’s own schedule, so check the DHI catalog for current tags before copying these.

What actually disappeared

The package-count reduction did not mostly consist of obscure OS packages. Instead many of the removed packages were from the npm toolchain itself, e.g. , , , etc. These packages are part of the standard Node.js image but the MCP server never runs npm in production, only . Thus they represent attack surface for code that never runs anyway, and a hardened base image removes them as a side effect of its minimal nature.

The rest was the Debian userland the server never touches at runtime: , , //, , , and .

Plan for debugging without a shell in production

Hardened runtime images are typically shipped without a shell but every major option here also ships a debug or development variant precisely so you're not left without one when you need it: distroless publishes tags with a busybox shell, Chainguard offers tags with a full toolchain, and Docker Hardened Images has variants we used exactly this variant for our own build stage, because Docker's instruction executes through a shell by default and the build stage needs to run . The practical takeaway isn't "accept no shell, ever" it's choosing a minimal variant for the production runtime and deliberately planning a separate debugging path in advance, rather than assuming the shell you're used to having will still be there when something breaks.

For Docker Hardened Images specifically, Docker Debug attaches a debugging toolkit to a running container without adding a shell to the image itself, so docker exec -it <container> sh failing is no longer a dead end.

The broader landscape, briefly

Google’s distroless images are built on top of Debian and are automatically updated to the latest Debian packages via pull requests to the distroless repository. Chainguard builds packages from source on top of its own distribution, Wolfi, and builds images daily with pinned versions of packages. Hardened versions of Docker images are built on top of the Debian or Alpine Linux distributions and are free and Apache 2.0 licensed as of the end of 2025. This means that, depending on your existing toolchain, the compliance requirements of your organization, and how much effort you are willing to invest in migrating, there is a hardened image provider that can fit your needs.

Why this is worth doing now

The container that needed hardening used to be almost always customer-facing. Increasingly, it's internal tooling too MCP servers, agent bridges, anything giving an AI system reach into company systems. Those containers carry real credentials and real API access, and in our own experience, this class of internal tooling hasn't gotten the same scanning rigor as public-facing services. That's the actual gap this exercise closed for us: not a security guarantee, but a measurable, documented reduction in attack surface for one of these newer, less-scrutinized internal services.

items.title: Implementing Transactional API Idempotency With Node.js and PostgreSQL
items.author: Douglas Matoso
items.content:
Idempotency keys are supposed to make retries safe: the client sends the same key on every attempt, and the server runs the operation once and replays the saved response after that. Most implementations keep the keys in Redis, next to the API, while the operation itself writes to a database. If the server crashes after the database write and before the key is updated, the two disagree.

In my guide to idempotency in APIs with Node.js, I build an wrapper for Express with an in-memory store and then a Redis store, and I mention this gap near the end: if the server dies after the work but before the response is saved, a retry can run the work again. This article picks up from there. I reproduce the double charge for real, and then close the gap by putting the key and the payment in the same PostgreSQL transaction.

Everything below was run with Node.js 24.21, Express 5.3.0, 8.23.1, the package 6.3.1, Redis 8.10.2 and PostgreSQL 18.6 (both in Docker), on Windows 11 with Git Bash, in November 2026. The output is copied from those runs.

I took the code from the guide as is: with the idempotent(store, handler) wrapper, with and a 60-second lock, and the that retries with the same key. The only change is that payments now go to a real table instead of an array:

CREATE TABLE payments (
  id uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  amount integer NOT NULL,
  status text NOT NULL,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

creates a connection pool:

import pg from 'pg'

export const pool = new pg.Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL })

And inserts the row, then does something slow, like sending the receipt email. To get a crash at exactly the wrong moment, I added a line that kills the process right after the when an environment variable is set. In real life this is a deploy, an out-of-memory kill or a pod being rescheduled:

async function createPayment(db, amount) {
  const { rows } = await db.query(
    `INSERT INTO payments (amount, status) VALUES ($1, 'succeeded')
     RETURNING id, amount, status`,
    [amount],
  )
  if (process.env.CRASH_AFTER_INSERT) process.exit(1) // simulate a crash
  await sleep(2000) // e.g. send the receipt email
  return rows[0]
}

app.post(
  '/payments',
  idempotent(redisStore, async (req) => {
    const payment = await createPayment(pool, req.body.amount)
    return { status: 201, body: payment }
  }),
)

Reproducing the double charge

I started the server with the crash flag and sent one request:

$ CRASH_AFTER_INSERT=1 node server-redis.js
$ curl -sS -X POST http://localhost:3000/payments \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: 7f9c2b1e-3d4a-4c6b-9e8f-1a2b3c4d5e6f" \
  -d '{"amount":4999}'
curl: (56) Recv failure: Connection was reset

The client got no answer. Here's what the crash left behind:

$ docker exec idem-pg psql -U postgres -c 'SELECT id, amount, status FROM payments'
                  id                  | amount |  status
--------------------------------------+--------+-----------
 3a1df61b-7a8c-4efe-a3ec-3b432f1ffb0c |   4999 | succeeded
(1 row)

$ docker exec idem-redis redis-cli GET "idem:POST:/payments:7f9c2b1e-3d4a-4c6b-9e8f-1a2b3c4d5e6f"
{"state":"processing","fingerprint":"2a9171e9d44f62b0d98368f20620dd1b0d7392d541b497bc93286e56789c6265"}
$ docker exec idem-redis redis-cli TTL "idem:POST:/payments:7f9c2b1e-3d4a-4c6b-9e8f-1a2b3c4d5e6f"
(integer) 59

The payment exists, but Redis still thinks the request is in progress, and it will keep thinking so for 59 more seconds. I restarted the server normally and retried with the same key:

HTTP/1.1 409 Conflict

{"error":"A request with this key is in progress"}

So far, so good: the wrapper did its job. Then I waited for the lock to expire and retried again:

HTTP/1.1 201 Created

{"id":"778a7a30-4b1b-4835-b0ce-f7c4411ac898","amount":4999,"status":"succeeded"}

$ docker exec idem-pg psql -U postgres -c 'SELECT id, amount, status FROM payments'
                  id                  | amount |  status
--------------------------------------+--------+-----------
 3a1df61b-7a8c-4efe-a3ec-3b432f1ffb0c |   4999 | succeeded
 778a7a30-4b1b-4835-b0ce-f7c4411ac898 |   4999 | succeeded
(2 rows)

That's two payments for one idempotency key. The lock expiration that frees a key after a crash is what lets the work run twice. The code does what it was written to do, but Redis and Postgres can't commit together, so the key says "not done" while the database says "done".

Put the key in the same database

If the operation's side effects are writes to your own Postgres, the fix is to store the key there too and do everything in one transaction: claim the key, insert the payment, save the response, commit. If the process dies at any point before , Postgres rolls back all of it, the key included. A retry then finds no key and no payment, and runs normally.

CREATE TABLE idempotency_keys (
  key text PRIMARY KEY,
  fingerprint text NOT NULL,
  status integer,
  body jsonb,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

and stay until the request finishes. And , a new wrapper with the same checks as the guide's (400 without a key, 422 for a different body, replay with ):

import { createHash } from 'node:crypto'

export function idempotentTx(pool, handler) {
  return async (req, res) => {
    const key = req.get('Idempotency-Key')
    if (!key) {
      return res.status(400).json({ error: 'Missing Idempotency-Key header' })
    }

    const storeKey = `idem:${req.method}:${req.path}:${key}`
    const fingerprint = createHash('sha256')
      .update(JSON.stringify(req.body ?? null))
      .digest('hex')

    const db = await pool.connect()
    try {
      await db.query('BEGIN')

      // claim the key: a duplicate waits here until the first transaction ends
      const claim = await db.query(
        `INSERT INTO idempotency_keys (key, fingerprint) VALUES ($1, $2)
         ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING`,
        [storeKey, fingerprint],
      )

      if (claim.rowCount === 0) {
        await db.query('ROLLBACK')
        const { rows } = await db.query(
          'SELECT fingerprint, status, body FROM idempotency_keys WHERE key = $1',
          [storeKey],
        )
        const saved = rows[0]
        if (saved.fingerprint !== fingerprint) {
          return res
            .status(422)
            .json({ error: 'Idempotency-Key reused with a different body' })
        }
        res.set('Idempotent-Replayed', 'true')
        return res.status(saved.status).json(saved.body)
      }

      // the handler writes with the same connection, in the same transaction
      const { status, body } = await handler(req, db)

      await db.query(
        'UPDATE idempotency_keys SET status = $2, body = $3 WHERE key = $1',
        [storeKey, status, body],
      )
      await db.query('COMMIT')
      res.status(status).json(body)
    } catch (err) {
      await db.query('ROLLBACK')
      throw err
    } finally {
      db.release()
    }
  }
}

The important detail is that the handler receives , the connection that holds the transaction, and must use it for its writes. If it used , the payment would be committed on another connection, outside the transaction, and we'd be back to two systems that commit separately.

The route only changes the wrapper and passes along:

app.post(
  '/payments',
  idempotentTx(pool, async (req, db) => {
    const payment = await createPayment(db, req.body.amount)
    return { status: 201, body: payment }
  }),
)

Notice there's no state anymore, and no lock with an expiration time. The uncommitted row is the lock, and it disappears when the transaction ends, whether it commits or the connection dies.

Same test, same flag, a new key:

$ curl -sS -X POST http://localhost:3000/payments \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: 0d8f6a52-91c4-4b1e-a7d3-5e2f8c9b4a10" \
  -d '{"amount":4999}'
curl: (56) Recv failure: Connection was reset

$ docker exec idem-pg psql -U postgres -c 'SELECT count(*) FROM payments' -c 'SELECT key, status FROM idempotency_keys'
 count
-------
     0
(1 row)

 key | status
-----+--------
(0 rows)

The into ran, but it was never committed. When the process died, its connection closed and Postgres threw the transaction away, so neither the payment nor the key exists. I restarted the server and retried with the same key, twice:

HTTP/1.1 201 Created

{"id":"e20ea825-9f99-4caf-9dfc-3c0d30fe4fa5","amount":4999,"status":"succeeded"}

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Idempotent-Replayed: true

{"id":"e20ea825-9f99-4caf-9dfc-3c0d30fe4fa5","amount":4999,"status":"succeeded"}

One payment in the table. The same key with returns , like in the guide. And no waiting for a lock to expire: the retry worked right after the restart.

What happens to a concurrent retry

With the Redis store, a retry that arrives while the first request is still running gets right away, and the client has to try again later. With Postgres, the second INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING sees a row with the same key that isn't committed yet, so it can't know whether that row will exist or not. It waits. When the first transaction commits, the does nothing and the wrapper replays the saved response. If the first one rolls back, the goes through and the retry does the work itself.

I sent request A, and request B with the same key 300 ms later:

A: HTTP 201 after 2.054941s
B: HTTP 201 after 1.744528s

B didn't get a . It sat there for about 1.7 seconds and then got A's response. The guide's retrying client shows the same thing: attempt 2 used to get , and now it gets the payment:

$ node client.js http://localhost:3000/payments
Attempt 1 failed: The operation was aborted due to timeout
Attempt 2: HTTP 201 {
  id: '7a45d43e-6fbc-43cf-a16c-1e0c1d5a284a',
  amount: 4999,
  status: 'succeeded'
}

For short operations that's nicer for the client. For long ones it's a problem: every waiting duplicate holds a connection from the pool, and has 10 by default. A client stuck in a retry loop could use up the pool by itself.

If you'd rather keep the , tell Postgres how long to wait. cancels a statement that waits too long for a lock, with SQLSTATE . limits it to the current transaction:

await db.query('BEGIN')
await db.query("SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '500ms'")

} catch (err) {
  await db.query('ROLLBACK')
  if (err.code === '55P03') {
    // lock_timeout: the first request still holds the key
    return res
      .status(409)
      .json({ error: 'A request with this key is in progress' })
  }
  throw err
}

B: HTTP 409 after 0.517783s
A: HTTP 201 after 2.048949s

And the guide's client is back to the behavior from the Redis version:

$ node client.js http://localhost:3000/payments
Attempt 1 failed: The operation was aborted due to timeout
Attempt 2 failed: HTTP 409
Attempt 3: HTTP 201 {
  id: '59522393-3398-4728-852b-29b6d2ce1ddb',
  amount: 4999,
  status: 'succeeded'
}
  • Side effects outside your database. A transaction can roll back rows, not a card charge at a payment provider or an email that was already sent. For those, pass the same key to the provider (the guide shows how with Stripe), and keep slow external calls out of the transaction, since the connection is held for as long as the transaction is open.
  • Postgres doesn't expire rows on its own. You need a scheduled job that deletes keys older than your retention window (24 hours is common), using .
  • As in the guide, put the user or account ID in , or two clients that happen to send the same key will see each other's responses.

With the key and the work in one transaction:

  1. A crash before leaves nothing behind, so a retry runs the operation once, right away, with no lock to wait out.
  2. A duplicate that arrives during the first request waits and gets the same response, or gets a if you set .
  3. The "processing" state and its expiration time are gone, because the uncommitted row does that job.

The trade-off is that it only works when the side effects live in the same database as the keys. When they don't, it doesn't matter where the keys live: you still need to pass the key downstream. The concepts this builds on (idempotent HTTP methods, the header draft, the fingerprint check and the Redis store) are in my step-by-step guide to idempotency keys in Node.js.

items.title: A Man In Denver Has Been Trapping Waymos
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: A bearded man with a brown ponytail has been on the hunt for Waymos in Denver, trapping the self-driving taxis so they can't pull away (source paywalled; alternative source) and hurling cartons of eggs at them, the police and company officials said. There have been at least 30 episodes of the egg attacks, according to Waymo, and a company investigator reported seven of them to the Denver police, all believed to be linked to the same man, according to a police report filed last month. [...] The man, who remains unidentified, stopped in front of the Waymo vans and S.U.V.s circulating in and around downtown Denver, according to the police report. Then, he removed orange cones from his car's trunk and placed them around the vehicles "to prevent the Waymo vehicle from moving," the report said. In some instances, the man threw eggs "while seated inside his vehicle" and at other times he "throws eggs at the Waymo vehicle after exiting his vehicle," the report said. The man then fled in a silver Toyota Corolla, which according to the report is part of a fleet of vehicles "able to be leased for Lyft drivers." Waymo said they had to temporarily pull the egged vehicles from service and spend about $2,000 on cleaning, though no permanent damage was reported.
 
Denver prosecutors declined to file criminal charges, deeming the case a civil matter, but are continuing to collect evidence and explore legal options to stop the behavior. The driver remains unidentified.

items.title: NYT Warns Photographers Not To Update Photoshop Over AI Features
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
The New York Times is instructing freelance photographers not to use Adobe Photoshop 2027 (version 28.0.0 and subsequent updates), warning that its new AI features operate "in ways that may not be apparent to users" and "can result in metadata identifying photographs as AI-generated." The Verge reports: It's not always clear which tools in Adobe's apps are AI-powered, and even some older options like automated selection tools may now be considered part of the AI suite. This can lead to photos ending up with metadata indicating they were edited with AI, which is a blunt way of describing what happened in post-production. For a newsroom like the Times, where photo editing is kept to a minimum, the metadata risks losing readers' trust.
 
Last year, the Times said that it does not "retouch or digitally manipulate" photos but may "make minimal adjustments to color to ensure we are accurately reproducing the image." In August, Adobe began rolling out support for C2PA metadata across its apps, which indicates whether an image is AI-generated or edited using AI features. The NYT is issuing its restriction to keep these tags from inadvertently appearing in its photos.

items.title: S&P Warns Nvidia's Board May Be Compromised
items.author: BeauHD
items.content: S&P Global Ratings has placed Nvidia's AA credit rating on downgrade watch, warning that Jensen Huang's departure and subsequent reinstatement as CEO exposed weaknesses in the company's corporate governance and board oversight. "We believe the long tenure of certain board members may have compromised their independence. The company's corporate governance practices may also not have kept pace with Nvidia's rapid growth and its role as a critical global technology enabler," the ratings agency said. Reuters reports: Nvidia currently has an 'AA' rating from S&P, which indicates a very strong capacity to meet financial commitments. The highest rating is 'AAA'. The agency said it could downgrade Nvidia within the next 90 days, but expects any potential downgrade to be limited to one notch, unless investigations and other disclosures harm the company's reputation or future business prospects.
