items.title: Does AI Really Need a Data Center? Lowdown Labs Bets on Efficient AI for Ordinary CPUs
items.author: Nica Furs
items.content:
Tech companies are spending heavily on new data centers to keep up with demand for artificial intelligence, and new campuses are often described by how many gigawatts of power it will draw. For most people outside the industry, AI means a chatbot run by one of a few large companies on a server farm somewhere far away. That setup comes with a heavy energy bill, and the usual industry answer to rising demand is to build more of the same.

Lowdown Labs, a Seattle startup founded by researchers and engineers from Caltech and Georgia Tech, is looking for the answer in software. The company builds AI models that need serious computing power to train but can run day to day on ordinary computers without graphics chips. Its first commercial product, the , is meant to show that this efficient AI approach can handle real business workloads at scale.

Why training and inference need different hardware

Every AI model goes through two stages. Training is when the model learns from large amounts of data, and it happens once or every so often. Inference is when the finished model does its job, such as recognizing an image or answering a question. Inference happens every time someone uses the model, so its energy cost keeps adding up long after training is over.

Lowdown Labs trains its models on high-performance machines, as the rest of the industry does. The difference starts at inference, which the company runs on commodity CPUs, the standard processors found in regular servers and laptops. Graphics processing units (GPUs), the chips that fill most AI data centers, are left out of this stage entirely.

To make that work, the team changed the math inside the model. The widely used Transformer architecture compares every part of the input with every other part, so its memory needs grow with the square of the input length. The company replaces this with Fourier encoders, which rely on a long-established technique called the Fast Fourier Transform, and with linear attention, whose memory needs grow in step with the input. In practice, doubling the length of the input roughly doubles the memory the model needs, where the standard approach would need about four times as much. The company sums up the result as AI that runs on watts instead of gigawatts.

FEVER is a computer vision model, meaning software that lets computers understand what is in a picture, combined with a database that stores and searches the results. According to the company, it indexes about 5 million photos a day. The same API also handles video and audio files alongside documents, and it removes duplicates as it goes. Teams can query the archive with keywords or SQL and send finished datasets to AI tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

FEVER runs in the customer's own cloud, so the files never leave the company's infrastructure and no user data is shared. Lowdown Labs positions it for three jobs:

  • Building in-house AI training datasets from large, messy collections of photos and videos.
  • Checking an archive for illicit or fraudulent images, which the company compares to running a Google search over your own files.
  • Letting staff or customers search a whole catalog in plain language, for example by typing "trendy blue jeans".

Many companies that need this kind of image and video dataset curation assume they have to build the system themselves. FEVER lets them skip that project, and the company says the total cost comes out 10 to 100 times lower than the alternatives.

Lowdown Labs sees FEVER as evidence that efficient AI can take on jobs usually left to the largest AI providers. Processing a steady stream of images and video is demanding work, and the company argues that doing it on modest hardware shows the same methods can go further.

The company's next step is a large language model (LLM), the type of model behind chatbots, that runs entirely without data centers. The company says it is close to good results and plans to release the model soon. A language model like that would let businesses and individuals run AI on hardware they already own and keep their data under their own control.

The company calls its goal responsible AI: models that people can manage and use safely, without the environmental cost of ever-larger server farms. For companies sitting on growing media archives, FEVER is the part of that plan they can put to work today.

items.title: AntSeed Review 2027: Cheapest Way to Run an OpenClaw & Hermes Agent 24/7 on Pay-Per-Request Model
items.author: Ishan Pandey
items.content:
AntSeed is a peer-to-peer market for AI inference that lets an always-on agent like OpenClaw or Hermes send every model call to the cheapest verified provider on the network. Instead of one company setting the price, independent providers list the same open models at their own prices, and a local proxy sends each request to the cheapest provider that meets the buyer's minimum trust score. AntSeed's own calculation for a coding agent's month of usage puts Claude Opus 5.5 at 93% below list price on its network and Claude Sonnet 5.5 at 89% below, based on advertised prices in mid-November 2026. For an agent that makes hundreds of calls a day, that difference compounds, which is why the model layer decides the cheapest way to run an AI agent 24/7.

Verdict: AntSeed is built for OpenClaw and Hermes users who run open models around the clock and want the model bill to fall through price competition. It asks for a little more setup than a hosted API, and it rewards that setup on every call.

is a peer-to-peer network for AI services. Providers announce their models and prices on a distributed hash table, the same kind of discovery system BitTorrent uses. Buyers run a local endpoint that finds those providers and sends requests to them over encrypted peer-to-peer connections. There is no central aggregator between buyer and provider.

AntSeed says the network offers more than 700 models, and its live count in mid-November 2026 was 703 models from 95 providers, including image and video models. The Antseed Foundation has raised $2.4M in a token round led by Spark Capital, with participation from Collider, DCG, North Island Ventures, Reciprocal Ventures, Relayer Capital, and Venice.ai.

The network is in real use. According to AntSeed's on-chain figures, it averaged about 31.7 billion tokens and 434,000 requests a day from 9 to 15 November 2026. In the 30 days to 15 November, 692 paying wallets paid about $76,800 to 104 different providers over that period. AntSeed notes that paid token counts are a lower bound, because they only include usage that buyers report on-chain.

How does AntSeed route requests?

Routing is the reason AntSeed suits a 24/7 agent. According to , the local proxy sends each request to the cheapest provider that meets the buyer's minimum trust score (60 out of 100 by default), unless the buyer pins a specific provider. Providers that are cooling down or have recently failed are moved down the list, so another provider takes the request.

For an always-on agent, this changes the cost model. A single-provider API charges one price for every call. On AntSeed, every call is a fresh choice among competing providers, so the agent pays the lowest price available at that moment for the model it asked for.

How to run OpenClaw or Hermes on AntSeed

The local endpoint speaks both the OpenAI and Anthropic APIs, so an agent connects to it the way it would connect to any compatible provider. The setup has four steps, followed by AntSeed's recommended gateway option.

Step 1: Install AntSeed on the agent's machine

Install the AntSeed command-line tool on the agent's machine with npm install -g @antseed/cli, which needs Node.js 20 or later. AntSeed also publishes an agent-readable setup skill, so an agent can follow the installation steps itself. On a personal computer, the AntSeed desktop app runs the same local endpoint.

Step 2: Start the local endpoint

Running antseed buyer start launches the local buyer proxy at http://127.0.0.1:8377/v1, which works only on the same machine as the agent. If your agent runs on a VPS, install AntSeed on the same server so the agent can reach the endpoint on localhost.

Step 3: Point the agent at the endpoint

For any OpenAI-compatible agent, set the base URL to the local endpoint and use the placeholder API key antseed-p2p, since the local endpoint does not validate one.

For OpenClaw, AntSeed's adds the antseed provider to ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json, after which a model can be selected with a command such as openclaw models set "antseed/kimi-k2.6", followed by openclaw gateway restart.

For Hermes, AntSeed is registered as a custom provider in ~/.hermes/config.yaml following AntSeed's , then Hermes is restarted to load it.

Step 4: Fund the balance for paid models

Providers are always paid per request in USDC on Base. The command-line proxy is funded with USDC only, and antseed buyer deposit shows the funding address. The gateway and the desktop app also take card top-ups of $1 to $200 where available, and no AntSeed account is needed for either.

AntSeed now recommends the gateway for agents. Run antseed gateway service install, then antseed gateway key create --label openclaw, and point the agent at http://localhost:8379/v1. Each agent gets its own key and budget. For OpenClaw without funds, the model antseed/@preset/openclaw tries free providers first. Some providers offer free models.

AntSeed has no subscription. The agent pays per request, at the price of the provider that serves it. The total depends on which models the agent uses and how many calls it makes.

Live prices are listed on , an independent tracker that lists network prices for each model next to its official API price. AntSeed's own calculation for a coding agent's month of 22 million input and 5.5 million output tokens shows the gap:

Across 192 models with a published list price, showed a median saving of 52% on 12 November 2026. AntSeed's figures use advertised prices and the cheapest provider that passes its default trust minimum, so they are not measured per request. Prices move as providers join and compete, so check the live rates before estimating a budget.

For a 24/7 agent, the per-call saving matters most on background traffic. OpenClaw's default heartbeat runs every 30 minutes, which is 48 model calls a day before the agent does any real work. Each of those calls goes to the cheapest qualifying provider.

It turns price into competition. The same open model can be served by several providers, and the agent pays the lowest qualifying price on each request rather than a fixed list price.

It keeps the agent unchanged. OpenClaw and Hermes keep their configuration, memory and tools. Only the model endpoint changes, and switching back is a matter of pointing the agent at a different base URL.

It adds resilience. Because many providers serve the same model, a provider that fails does not stop the agent. The proxy moves on to another one.

It scales with the network. As more providers join, the price competition for popular models increases.

Where it is less convenient

AntSeed runs locally. The endpoint has to run next to the agent, which is one more process to keep alive on the server. A hosted aggregator such as OpenRouter needs nothing running on your machine.

Prices vary by provider and over time. That is the point of the market, but it means the cost of a given model is a live figure, not a fixed list price.

The model range depends on providers. Popular open models are well covered, while a niche model may have few sellers or none.

Beyond agents: AntSeed's gateway for AI apps

The same network also serves teams building AI apps. AntSeed's sits in front of an existing OpenAI- or Anthropic-based app through the Chat Completions, Responses and Messages APIs, so switching means changing the API address, key and model rather than rewriting code. It can run on a developer's computer or on a server.

What the gateway adds is control. Each app gets its own key, and spending limits can be set per key, per team member or per workspace, by day, week, month or lifetime. Keys can allow only certain models, allow or block certain providers, and cap the price per million input, output and cached input tokens, as well as the price per image. Provider ranking and fallback rules are configurable too. With automatic routing, a request that fails with a retryable error can move to another provider before streaming starts. Balances can be topped up by card or USDC, with no AntSeed account needed. For a 24/7 agent that has become part of a product, such as a support agent, this is the layer that shows what each app costs and stops one runaway app from draining the budget for the rest.

AntSeed is the strongest choice for builders running OpenClaw, Hermes or another OpenAI-compatible agent around the clock on open models, who want the lowest per-request price and are comfortable running one local endpoint. Teams shipping AI apps can put the same network behind each app through the gateway, with a key and a budget for every app.

It is less suited to someone who wants a single hosted API key with nothing to install, or who needs a model that few providers serve.

Frequently asked questions

What's the cheapest way to run an AI agent 24/7?

Host the agent on a low-cost or free server and keep the model bill down, since it is usually the bigger cost. Running open models through AntSeed sends each call to the cheapest verified provider on the network. Routing heartbeats to a small or free model and lengthening the heartbeat interval cuts background spend further.

Does AntSeed work with OpenClaw and Hermes?

Yes. OpenClaw and Hermes both have maintained AntSeed setup skills and integration guides. Any other agent that speaks the OpenAI or Anthropic API can connect by pointing its custom provider settings at the local endpoint.

Is AntSeed cheaper than OpenRouter?

OpenRouter passes through each provider's list price, charging a fee when you buy credits. On AntSeed, independent providers compete on price for every request. The independent tracker AntSeedStats showed a median saving of 52% against list prices across 192 models on 12 November 2026. The saving for your agent depends on the models it uses.

Can AntSeed run on a VPS?

Yes. Install AntSeed on the same server as the agent and start the local endpoint there, so the agent reaches it on localhost. This is the simplest setup for a 24/7 agent.

How do I pay for AntSeed?

Providers are paid per request in USDC on Base. The command-line proxy takes USDC only, while the gateway and the desktop app also accept card top-ups of $1 to $200, handled by Crossmint and not available in every region. No AntSeed account is needed. Some providers offer free models. There is no subscription.

Can I use AntSeed for an AI app, not just an agent?

Yes. AntSeed's works with existing OpenAI- and Anthropic-based apps by changing the API address, key and model. Each app gets its own key and spending limit, and requests are routed across the same competing providers that serve agents.

items.title: When Everyone Looks Qualified, Who Actually Is?
items.author: Nick Garvin
items.content:
We've spent decades building systems that recognize achievement. AI is forcing us to reconsider how we recognize capability.

Spend enough time around startups and you'll recognize the pattern.

An ambitious founder. A compelling pitch deck. A product roadmap promising to transform an industry.

Investors get interested. People start talking. Talented employees leave secure jobs to join something that feels like the next big thing.

The company begins hiring.

And somewhere along the way, the ability to tell a convincing story starts getting confused with the ability to deliver one.

Strategy meetings fill with ambitious promises. Deadlines slip. The people doing the difficult work begin losing confidence.

Eventually, the distance between the pitch and the product becomes impossible to ignore.

By then, good people have left, teams have burned out, and trust has eroded.

There's a particular kind of bullshit that thrives in environments where confidence is mistaken for competence.

Persuasion, of course, is an essential part of entrepreneurship. Great founders attract talent, capital, and belief long before their vision becomes reality. Some of the world's most successful companies began with ideas that seemed almost impossible.

The trouble begins when the ability to sell the vision outpaces the ability to execute it, and nobody recognizes the difference until the consequences arrive.

AI is making that distinction even harder.

In April 2026, recruitment firm Robert Half reported something revealing about Australian hiring managers.

There's an uncomfortable contradiction here.

Employers increasingly expect people to work with AI, while the same technology is making it harder to determine what those people can actually do.

A candidate can arrive with an impressive résumé, a sophisticated portfolio, a working prototype, and a beautifully articulated strategy.

Some will have exercised extraordinary judgment in creating that work. Others may understand very little of what they're presenting.

And from the finished product alone, distinguishing between them is becoming increasingly difficult.

We've encountered versions of this problem in education for decades.

Two students earn the same grade. One has developed deep understanding through experimentation, feedback, and revision. The other has learned how to satisfy the assessment.

The number looks identical.

The learning behind it may be very different.

Now imagine those students graduating, entering the workforce, and eventually founding or leading organizations.

A degree opens a door. A résumé earns an interview. A portfolio demonstrates experience.

But what happens when the signals we've traditionally trusted become less revealing about the capabilities people have actually developed?

Consider a startup founder evaluating a developer with an impressive portfolio.

Three polished applications.

Clean interfaces. Working demonstrations. A GitHub profile filled with activity.

Everything looks promising.

The founder could ask which AI tools the candidate uses, how quickly they built the applications, or what frameworks they know.

But imagine asking them to show the part that almost failed.

The architectural decision they got wrong.

The vulnerability they discovered.

The solution AI confidently recommended that they eventually rejected.

Now ask them to explain what happened.

What made them question the original approach? What evidence changed their mind? What would they do differently today?

That conversation might reveal more about their capabilities than the finished portfolio ever could.

AI is making it cheaper to look capable.

The cost of mistaking appearance for ability remains extraordinarily high.

There's a phrase from Web3 that feels especially relevant here.

In blockchain, it refers to a mechanism for validating computational work and helping secure a network. I'm borrowing the phrase as a metaphor for something more human.

What if we became better at recognizing the thinking behind what people produce?

Consider the founder who abandoned a promising pitch after discovering that customers didn't actually need the product.

Or the designer who rejected their most visually impressive prototype because user testing exposed a fundamental flaw.

Or the graduate who challenged an AI-generated analysis, discovered that its assumptions were wrong, and rebuilt the argument from the evidence.

There's something revealing about the work people decide against doing.

The ideas they abandon. The shortcuts they refuse. The assumptions they reconsider.

Those decisions can reveal judgment, adaptability, and intellectual honesty.

And they rarely appear on a résumé.

This is where portfolios, meaningful data, and visible learning become valuable.

Imagine students graduating with evidence of projects, demonstrated skills, feedback, and how their thinking developed over time.

Founders presenting validated experiments and customer evidence alongside projections.

Employees being recognized for the problems they've solved, the independence they've developed, and the contributions they've made.

These records could tell richer stories about human capability.

Of course, AI can also manufacture convincing portfolios, reflections, and accounts of someone's process. Credible evidence still requires verification, authentic demonstrations, and the ability to apply what we've learned.

There may be a useful role here for portable digital credentials, including Web3 approaches that help establish where evidence originated and who verified it.

But the meaning of that evidence will always require judgment.

I think this is the deeper question.

Every system of recognition shapes behavior.

Schools reward grades. Companies reward performance. Startups reward growth, momentum, and the ability to attract belief.

All of those signals tell us something.

But as AI makes impressive work easier to produce, the decisions behind that work may become increasingly important.

The questions someone asked. The assumptions they challenged. The mistakes they recognized. The ideas they had the judgment to abandon.

And imagine what might change if we became better at recognizing those moments.

A school that helps students see how their thinking has developed.

A founder who values the candidate who can explain a failed project as thoughtfully as a successful one.

An organization that recognizes the employee who quietly prevents a costly mistake.

An investor who looks beyond the pitch to understand the evidence and judgment behind it.

These are choices about what we value, what we measure, and what we encourage people to become.

They also connect to the central idea behind : as intelligent machines become more capable, human judgment, independence, and responsibility become increasingly important.

Perhaps those are the qualities our systems should become better at recognizing.

Because when everyone looks qualified, the most interesting question may be:

Can you show me the thinking behind what you've built?

items.title: I Built a React Tool to Trace Where a 464 ms Click Spent Its Time
items.author: Aditya Reddy
items.content:
I clicked Log in on a demo page. Chrome measured 464 ms from the click to the next paint. That was the page’s Interaction to Next Paint (INP) at the time. Okay, so the click was slow. I still needed to figure out where the time went.

So I built react-inp-blame. It lines up the browser’s interaction timings with what React committed. The login report showed 405 ms of processing. It leaned toward the click handler because only two components re-rendered.

464 ms click on button "login" in SignInPage. The onClick handler or React's render of
SignInPage most likely took the 405 ms, the handler the likelier: React re-rendered only
2 components.

I started it on September 12, 2026. 0.1.0 was on npm five days later and 1.0.0 came out on October 10. No runtime dependencies, MIT license. Everything I show below runs on the live demo, so you can go click the same buttons.

On most pages, INP is the latency of the longest interaction. On busier pages it drops one high outlier for every 50 interactions. Chrome’s tools and web-vitals break the interaction down into input delay, processing and presentation.

What usually makes it long

From the press until the first event handler starts

Something else hogging the main thread

The event handlers themselves

Your handler code, and in React, the render it triggers

From the end of the handlers until the next paint

Style, layout and paint work

Which is useful, up to a point. In a React app "processing" is your onClick plus React's render plus whatever effects ran along the way, all lumped together, and the thing you clicked is a button nested a few components deep. When you actually sit down to fix it you want something smaller and more annoying. Which component? Which handler? How many renders? Was it even React?

React DevTools can answer some of it, if you had the profiler recording at the moment the slow click happened. Usually you didn't.

What it looks like on a slow sign-in page

The demo is a fake photo app called Framely with a sign-in page that has a few realistic mistakes baked in. Nothing leaves the page, the sign-in is simulated.

After the sign-in, a small dark badge in the bottom left corner shows the page's INP so far. It's green at 200 ms or under, amber up to 500 and red above that.

Click the badge and you get a panel of the recent slow interactions. Click a row and it opens up with the full explanation. My run for this article had 24 interactions in it, 15 key presses in the email field, 8 in the password field, and the one click.

The typing shows a different problem. Each key press in the email field re-rendered 1,004 components, 1,000 of them PostTile cards inside a FeedPreview that sits next to the form and has nothing to do with the email. The slowest key press took 232 ms and the typical one 160. The password field went the other way. Hardly anything rendered there, the time was in its own onChange handler, and the slowest press was 168 ms.

Then there's the second half of the login story, and honestly it's the part I care about most. React rendered again 274 ms after the screen had already updated, 256 components this time and most of them PhotoTile. INP doesn't count that render at all, cause it happened after the paint the click was waiting on. Whether it really belongs to the click is a harder question, I'll get to that.

How a click turns into a report

Funny thing is the browser and React already know all of this between them. They just don't share.

Event Timing gives me the interaction ID and its timing. The Long Animation Frames API records the scripts in a long frame and their forced style and layout time. For the React side I listen to the same developer tools hook that React DevTools uses. After a commit, the library walks the fiber tree and counts what rendered.

Matching them up is where it got hard. The library keeps its last eight inputs and uses event timestamps to associate commits with an interaction. A render that lands after the next paint is listed as a follow-up with its own timing. The report leaves its trigger open when the timing is the only evidence.

None of this is a stable React API, so the library checks what it reads and fails closed. If react-dom is outside 17 to 19, or the fiber tree looks different from what it expects, it switches that part off, warns once, and keeps reporting, just without component names.

Eight slow buttons on the demo

The demo also has an anti-pattern lab. It's eight slow interactions, each one built around one specific mistake, and a fast one as the control. I ran every scenario once on the live site, production build, and wrote down what the library said.

Every section rebuilt from scratch during render. 251 components inside SlowRender, mostly Section

Layout effects write a style, then read a size. 881 ms of forced style and layout, PriceTicker ×400

One class change restyles 30,000 cells. 773 ms updating the screen, browser work, no script

3,000 rows re-render on each key. 1,441 components inside BigList, mostly Row

Context value is a new object every render. 801 components, 800 LineItem inside OrderSummary

Input state lives above a heavy sidebar. 602 components, 600 NavItem inside Sidebar

The click handler burns 120 ms, nothing renders. The onClick handler, 120 ms

An effect sets more state after the click commits. A 401-component render 100 ms after the paint

Nothing, it's the control. No report, nothing stood out

Same nine interactions in the chart below, split by phase. Six are mostly "working", and that's the phase where a component or handler name is actually useful. Restyle storm is nearly all "updating the screen", where a React name won't help you at all.

When React isn't the slow part

I kept layout thrash in the lab cause it fooled me first. It looks exactly like a React problem. 400 rows, each one sets a style in a layout effect and then reads its own size back, and the browser has to redo layout 400 times inside a single commit. In the Performance panel it's one big purple and yellow block and you'd blame React for it.

Without the long-frame timing, the report would put roughly 1.1 seconds under processing. With it, I can see how much the browser spent recalculating styles and layout. Here’s what the report said.

1128 ms click on button "trigger" in LayoutThrash. Of the 1090 ms it took to handle the click,
the browser spent 881 ms recalculating styles and layout, leaving 209 ms for React's render
and commit, its layout effects, this library's read of what React rendered and the click
handler together.

Restyle storm goes one step further, there's basically no script in it. React renders a single component. Then one class change makes the browser restyle 30,000 cells, and that alone is 773 ms of "updating the screen" after the handler is long done (735 ms of it is the browser's own main thread work). No component name helps here. You fix it with fewer cells or CSS containment and React doesn't come into it.

Handler hog is the boring one and I like it for that. The onClick burns 120 ms, React renders nothing, and the report says so in one line. Nobody goes digging through the component tree for a render that never happened.

The render INP doesn't count

Cascading effect has an INP of 16 ms. Any dashboard would call that a perfect click.

Here's what's really going on. The click commits a tiny change, an effect picks it up and sets more state, and React renders again, 401 components this time, about 100 ms after the screen already updated. INP stops at the next paint, so it stops right before the expensive bit and never sees it.

I got the wording of this note wrong at first. Up to 0.25 it said people still wait for that render, which sounds right until you run it on a real app. On hyperdx, one of the two apps it was graded on, the render after a click was more than once a live tail's timer or a route change, nothing to do with the click. So from 0.26.0 the note only says INP doesn't count it and what started it can't be told. You still get the count and the time, it just doesn't pin it on a click it may not belong to.

Setting it up in Next.js or Vite

One package, and on most apps one line in the build config. Vite:

// vite.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from "vite";
import react from "@vitejs/plugin-react";
import { inpBlame } from "react-inp-blame/vite";

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [react(), inpBlame({ runtime: { overlay: true } })],
});

Next.js 14.2 or later wraps the config instead:

// next.config.ts
import type { NextConfig } from "next";
import { withInpBlame } from "react-inp-blame/next";

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {};

export default withInpBlame(nextConfig, { runtime: { overlay: true } });

Next.js 15.3 to 16.2 want one more export in instrumentation-client.ts. The wrapper keeps printing that line at you until the file has it, which is annoying on purpose. React Router in framework mode, Remix, TanStack Start and Astro all write their own HTML, so each gets its own short setup in the docs.

Both plugins only run in development unless you say otherwise. With the defaults a production build gets nothing from them (on Next.js 15.3 to 16.2 the extra export stays in, as an empty function).

CI covers react-dom 17.0.2 up to 19.3.0 plus React canary, Next.js 14.2.35 up to 16.3.5 plus canary, and Vite 6.4, 7.3 and 8.3. It also installs the packed tarball into fresh apps from , , TanStack Start's CLI and , then checks that a slow click there still gets blamed on the right component. That last part caught more bugs than the unit tests did.

Sending the blame where your INP already goes

Most teams already ship INP somewhere and I didn't want to replace that. The web-vitals attribution build keeps doing the measuring and this adds the React part on top. The lightest setup doesn't even need the runtime on the page, only the build step that keeps component names around:

import { onINP } from "web-vitals/attribution";
import { generateTarget } from "react-inp-blame/web-vitals";

onINP((metric) => console.log(metric), { generateTarget });

You need web-vitals 5.1 or later for that. If you want the full report, the docs have the path, sent on to Sentry or GA4.

There's also , still experimental. It adds the blame to the INP event an OpenTelemetry web vitals pipeline already sends, as attributes, so you can group and filter on it in Honeycomb, Elastic, Embrace or Grafana Faro. It doesn't import anything from OpenTelemetry or a vendor SDK. Experimental just means the attribute names could still change in a minor release, cause OpenTelemetry's browser conventions have no field yet for an interaction's target or a component.

A tool for slow clicks that makes clicks slower would be a bad joke. Every report carries , the library's own time for that interaction, so I couldn't really hide from it even if I wanted to.

The repo's numbers are 30 fresh page loads per scenario on two of the heaviest demo scenarios, a click that re-renders 801 components and a key press that re-renders 1,441:

In my own sign-in run for this article the 24 reports cost 0.1 to 3.2 ms each. The one outlier was the first key press on the page at 12 ms. Lab scenarios came in at 0.5 to 5.6 ms, one interaction each.

Size is the other cost if you turn it on in production:

, everything that loads with the page

The badge and panel, loaded only when shown

react-inp-blame/web-vitals, on top of

, on top of

35.8 KB gzip is real weight. That's why production is opt-in with a , and why the web-vitals path with no runtime exists at all.

The demo's header says "It can be wrong". I put that there and I meant it.

Treat a component name as a lead. In a production React build, the library uses component counts because it lacks render durations. The login report hedged between the handler and the render for that reason. Forced layout attribution also depends on the browser exposing Long Animation Frames.

Before 1.0 I set a bar for myself, at least 38 right and at most 6 wrong out of 62 verdicts on apps it had never seen. 0.25.0 got graded on two real open-source apps, hyperdx and kaneo. It got 8 right, 35 wrong and 19 misleading. So no, the bar isn't met, and the 1.0.0 changelog says that in plain words. What 1.0 promises is the API and the report shape, the fields keep their meaning through 1.x. Accuracy isn't part of that promise yet.

The next round is five everyday open-source React apps, Actual, myfin, Kresus, Manage My Damn Life and Reactive Resume. The protocol freezes the test cases before anyone looks at what the library says about them. Their integrations are still being built, so no results yet. If it blames the wrong thing on your app there's an issue form just for that, and honestly those reports help more than anything else.

Quickest way is the demo at reactinpblame.com. Everything on it is slow on purpose. Click around, read what the badge blames, then open the Performance panel in DevTools and check it, the library draws its own track there next to React's.

npm install react-inp-blame

Add the Vite plugin or the Next.js wrapper from above, restart the dev server and click the slowest thing you know about. Code, docs and known limits are on GitHub, and the package is on npm.

items.title: When AI Localization Translates a Promise You Cannot Keep
items.author: Pratik Thakker
items.content:
Hero illustration. Original AI-assisted illustration created for this article.

The translated page reads beautifully. The call to action works. The search annotations pass a technical check.

The page also promises a product feature that is not available in the reader's market.

Translation quality did not prevent the failure because the failure was not linguistic. A commercial claim crossed a regional boundary without being checked against regional facts.

I would treat AI localization as a release process for a local promise, not merely a process for producing text in another language. Fluency, product accuracy, technical delivery, and search configuration need separate checks.

Language and market are different dimensions

A language can serve several markets. A market can require several languages. Neither alone determines product eligibility, currency, commercial terms, or the correct sales destination.

Start by identifying the intended audience precisely enough for the decision. A Spanish-language educational article may serve readers across regions, while a product offer may require market-specific availability and terms.

Do not create unnecessary regional copies merely because a localization tool can generate them. Each additional version creates a maintenance obligation and another place where a promise can drift.

Conversely, do not force materially different offers into one universal translated page. If the underlying product or commercial facts differ, the content architecture needs to preserve that difference rather than hide it in a vague footnote.

The proposed design is a matrix of language, market, product scope, and intended action. It is not a claim that every company needs a separate URL for every combination. The right structure depends on the actual differences that readers need to understand.

Divide the source into shared claims and local facts

A shared claim might explain a general workflow or product concept. A local fact might state an available payment method, support arrangement, product edition, price, tax treatment, or delivery condition.

Keep local facts in a reviewed source of record rather than asking the translation model to infer them. A model can preserve approved values or flag missing ones; it should not choose a plausible regional offer because the source page lacks detail.

For each consequential fact, record its owner, effective date, scope, and review condition. Product marketing may own feature descriptions, while finance or the relevant commercial team owns approved pricing. Legal terms require the appropriate review rather than a linguistic approximation.

Do not confuse a disclaimer with a correction. A large promise at the top of a page remains misleading if a small note below quietly withdraws it for most readers.

The local version should state the applicable promise clearly where the reader makes the decision. If the correct fact is unknown, hold the affected claim or action until it can be verified.

A fictional page that passes translation review

Imagine a software company translating a page from English into German. The source says the product includes a particular payment capability. The capability is available only in selected markets and editions.

The translator preserves the sentence accurately. The local page is therefore faithful to the source and still wrong for part of its intended audience.

A better workflow attaches eligibility conditions to the claim before translation. The German page can then use the approved local statement or omit the unsupported promise. A language reviewer should not be expected to discover product entitlement rules from prose alone.

Now add a displayed price. Replacing a dollar sign with a euro sign is not currency conversion, local pricing approval, or tax treatment. Even a correctly formatted number can communicate the wrong commercial offer.

This is a constructed example, not a report about a particular product. It shows why translation accuracy and local business accuracy need independent sign-off. Neither check can safely stand in for the other.

A local promise needs three independent checks. Original AI-assisted illustration created for this article.

It does not decide the business value being formatted. A formatting function does not set a local price, apply an exchange-rate policy, or determine which taxes belong in a quoted offer.

Keep value calculation, commercial approval, and presentation separate. Test dates, percentages, units, ranges, and decimal precision as well as currency. A decimal or date ambiguity can alter an implementation instruction even when the surrounding translation is clear.

Do not rely only on screenshots. Validate the underlying structured values and the resulting visible text. A page can look plausible while its downloadable document, form confirmation, or checkout uses a different amount.

For technical content, preserve units explicitly. A translated performance claim needs the original measurement basis and conditions, not merely a localized numeral. If the source lacks that context, localization should reveal the gap rather than make the claim sound more authoritative.

Search annotations solve a different problem

The implementation should reflect actual alternatives and follow documented requirements, including reciprocal relationships where applicable. A technically correct annotation does not verify the offer or guarantee that a particular URL will appear for every user.

This is why an SEO checklist and a product-accuracy checklist must remain separate. Correct search signals can help describe the site's structure. They cannot repair an unavailable feature, an incorrect price, or an unsupported regional claim.

Do not manufacture regional pages with only a translated heading and unchanged main content. The visible content should be useful for the audience the page claims to serve, not merely a technical entry in an alternate-language set.

HTML language serves people and software too

That supports processing and accessibility. It is not identical to Google's use of visible content to determine page language, nor is it a replacement for localized-version annotations.

Keep these mechanisms distinct in review. The document language, visible language, alternative-page relationships, and commercial market can each be correct or incorrect independently.

Test navigation, form labels, validation messages, and confirmation screens, not only the article body. A reader should not encounter a translated promise followed by an unexplained language switch at the action point.

Also provide a usable way to choose another language or market where appropriate. A visitor's location does not necessarily establish their language preference or purchasing entity. Avoid trapping people in an inferred version that they cannot change.

Give AI a constrained localization task

A useful instruction identifies the audience, terminology, approved claims, immutable values, and unresolved local facts. Ask the system to flag conflicts rather than resolve them creatively.

For example, it can preserve an approved product name, translate an explanatory paragraph, and return a review note that the payment-method statement lacks a verified regional version. That is more useful than a fluent guess.

Separate language suggestions from factual edits. A reviewer should be able to see whether the model changed style, altered a number, removed a qualification, or introduced a new capability claim.

Use a glossary, but do not treat it as complete proof of quality. The same term can require different phrasing in a user interface, technical article, and legal document. Context and qualified human review still matter.

Back-translation can reveal some differences, but it is not a complete validation method. A model can translate an incorrect promise consistently in both directions. The factual source must be checked independently of linguistic consistency.

Run a release test across the whole journey

A locale release card can make the review concrete:

  • language, intended market, product edition, and purchasing context.
  • approved values and claim identifiers the translation must preserve.
  • unavailable capabilities, approved local pricing, and the correct action destination.
  • terminology, meaning, and material qualifications checked by an appropriately qualified reviewer.
  • visible copy, document language, alternate-version relationships, forms, and confirmation pages tested.
  • version, reviewer, effective date, unresolved holds, and the earlier version it replaces.

This is a proposed review artifact, not a requirement to expand a simple educational page into a large approval system. Apply greater scrutiny where an incorrect local promise could cause a consequential decision, and keep the process lighter where the content makes no regional commercial claim.

Choose representative page types and high-risk claims. Verify the approved local facts, visible copy, metadata, language declarations, alternative links, forms, downloadable assets, and final action destination.

Include negative cases. What happens when a capability is unavailable in the selected market? Does the page say so clearly, or does it continue to offer a misleading action? What happens when the local price has not been approved?

Test mobile layouts and text expansion. A qualification that is present but clipped, hidden, or separated from the promise may fail the reader even though a text comparison says it exists.

Record the review scope. One reviewed page does not validate an entire language site. A translation vendor's approval of wording does not establish that the checkout or campaign destination matches the offer.

The release decision should state which locales and page versions were verified, which remain held, and who owns unresolved factual questions. A batch status of translated is not a sufficient readiness state.

Maintain the promise after publication

When a shared source changes, identify the local versions and derivative campaigns that depend on the changed claim. Do not blindly overwrite every locale with a new translation if the local product facts differ.

Classify the change. A corrected typo, a new feature entitlement, and a revised price require different review paths. Some updates can propagate mechanically; others require a local decision before release.

Keep an effective-date record so the team can explain which version a reader encountered. If an earlier page was materially incorrect, review the appropriate correction and customer communication process rather than simply replacing the file and forgetting it.

Useful measures include unresolved local facts, stale versions awaiting review, broken alternative relationships, and mismatches between the page and its action destination. These are process indicators, not promises of ranking or revenue improvement.

AI makes producing another language version easier. The durable advantage is keeping each version connected to a promise the business can actually fulfill. Fluent translation opens the conversation. Accurate local facts are what allow the company to stand behind it.

items.title: I Built a Tool That Lets You Work on Multiple Projects in One AI Environment
items.author: w4p
items.content:
Use separate MCP endpoints to give each project its own services, then switch access without rebuilding your setup.

An online store has an order-status bug. A booking service has an availability problem. You want an AI assistant to investigate both, in separate conversations, while you review the results in the same development environment.

Opening another chat is easy. Keeping the tools attached to each project understandable takes more care. Both projects might use PostgreSQL and Redis. Both might have tables called . A tool named “query database” says very little about which application it can reach.

The setup in this walkthrough gives each project a named access path: one MCP endpoint for the store, another for the booking service. Both can stay available while work runs in parallel. Each also has a switch for temporarily stopping access, without deleting its configuration.

I build GateRook, the application used below. The screenshots show a local development build with fictional project data.

Separate the conversation from the service access

There are two things to organize when working on several projects with AI.

The first is the working context: the repository, instructions, conversation history, and task. Give each project its own workspace and conversation in your AI application.

The second is access to external services. The store needs its orders database and cache. The booking service needs its reservations database and availability cache. These are different resources even when they use the same technology.

MCP provides the connection between an AI application and tools. Its architecture allows a host application to connect to multiple servers; it does not prescribe how that application manages the model's context. That distinction matters here. MCP architecture overview

In GateRook, an endpoint is one MCP URL with its own selected connections, tool modes, and tokens. For this example, the layout is:

The same AI application can be configured with both endpoint URLs. Calls through use the store's configured services; calls through use the booking service's configured services.

That does automatically bind a particular chat to an endpoint. If an AI client exposes both endpoints globally, both may be available in either conversation. Use its project-level configuration when you need project-specific tool availability.

Give each project a small set of connections

Start by creating two endpoints in GateRook: and . Use names that identify the project and environment before any tool call happens.

Create the database and cache connections for each project. In the connection wizard's endpoint step, add and only to . Add and only to .

Then open Overview and select each endpoint. This is a useful check: does the list of services match the project you think you are working on?

Keep the underlying credentials scoped too. The two demo database connections use separate PostgreSQL roles with read access to their respective project tables. GateRook's connection test reported access and no table ownership or privilege.

This matters because an endpoint's tool policy and a database role govern different parts of a request. An approval in the gateway cannot grant a database privilege the role does not have. PostgreSQL documents these permissions separately, including , , , and . PostgreSQL privileges

For an investigation, enable the reads you need and review the write-capable tools. You can leave mutations behind approval or turn them off for that endpoint. Avoid giving a debugging session an administrator account just because it is convenient to configure.

Connect both endpoints to the same AI application

From Overview, select , choose , and follow the setup for your client. Review the configuration change before saving it. Repeat from for the same client.

For the local Cursor example, this produces two server entries, and , pointing to different endpoint URLs. Complete any enable or restart step requested by the client before using the tools.

Choose the configuration scope deliberately. Cursor supports project configuration in and global configuration in . Global entries are available across projects, so adding two global entries is a convenient shared setup, not a per-project access restriction. For project-specific availability, configure only the appropriate endpoint in each workspace and remove any global duplicate that exposes the other project. Keep literal tokens out of committed configuration. Cursor MCP documentation

The screenshots show configured access in GateRook. The connection map is not a display of live agent traffic.

Run two conversations with explicit tasks

With both endpoints enabled, keep a store conversation and a booking conversation open. Each should identify the project, the allowed endpoint, and the expected result.

Work on the online store. Use the shop-dev endpoint and shop-db connection. Read the orders schema and summarize order counts by status. Do not change data. Include the connection name in your result.

Work on the booking service. Use the booking-dev endpoint and booking-db connection. Read the reservations schema and summarize reservations by status. Do not change data. Include the connection name in your result.

These are example tasks you can reproduce with the demo's data. They give you something concrete to review: which service was used, what was read, and whether the answer addresses the correct application.

Explicit instructions help the agent choose tools, but they are not an access-control mechanism. Pair them with the workspace configuration and endpoint permissions described above.

This follows a useful theme in Alex Cloudstar's HackerNoon account of an AI coding workflow: write the constraints before asking the agent to work. Here, those constraints include the service access available to each task.

Switch off a project when you stop using it

Parallel work needs both endpoints available. At other times, you may want to concentrate on the store and temporarily stop new requests to the booking services.

Turn off on . GateRook preserves the endpoint's tool modes, tokens, and settings, while blocking new service operations through that endpoint. stays enabled.

Turn it back on when you need that project again. There is no need to recreate the connections or replace the endpoint URL.

The switch applies to every client using that endpoint. If another conversation is actively investigating the booking service, pausing also blocks its new service requests. Treat this as a shared access control, not a private switch for the chat you happen to be viewing.

Also, do not assume switching off cancels an operation already in progress. The useful guarantee for this workflow is control over subsequent requests.

Switch off one connection when the rest should stay available

Sometimes the database is still useful but the cache is not. Perhaps you are checking whether an answer can be derived entirely from persisted records.

Turn off and leave on. The endpoint stays enabled, and the database remains available under its existing rules.

The two controls have different scopes:

New service operations through that endpoint, across all its connections

New operations on that connection across every endpoint that uses it

Whether a particular tool is allowed, requires approval, or is off for that endpoint

In this demo, each connection belongs to one project endpoint. If you later share a connection between endpoints, its connection switch affects all of them. Use endpoint-specific tool modes when the restriction should apply to only one access path.

An off connection may still be discoverable, allowing the AI to ask you to enable it. Off means operations are blocked; it does not necessarily mean the client removes every reference to the service.

Keep the boundaries visible

Before starting a task, check the workspace, endpoint, and enabled services. When reviewing a result, check which connection supplied the data. When putting a project aside, decide whether its endpoint should remain available to other ongoing work.

Keep the limits of this arrangement clear. Switching access does not erase information already in a conversation. GateRook governs requests routed through it; an agent's separate shell tools or direct credentials are outside that path. And although service credentials stay in GateRook, tool results can still enter the AI application's context and reach its model provider.

The practical benefit is a setup you can inspect and change quickly: two project contexts in one AI environment, two named service-access paths, and controls for pausing either a whole project or one connection. When both projects are active, leave both available. When the task narrows, narrow the access with it.

items.title: Physicists Send an Unblockable Message Using Gravity
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Longtime Slashdot reader fahrbot-bot shares a report from Phys.org: University of Queensland researchers have used gravity to transmit a message through a brick wall using an elevator and a sensitive gravimeter. The unusual experiment took place in UQ's Parnell Building, where the team of physicists sent the elevator back and forth between two levels, moving its 1.8 metric ton (4,000 pound) counterweight between positions representing binary 0 and 1. A gravimeter in an adjacent bathroom detected the changes in the gravitational field and translated the message into a single word, "Gravity." The research has been published in Science Advances.
 
"Unlike the electromagnetic signals used in modern wireless communication, a gravitational signal cannot simply be screened out by placing ordinary material in its path," [said Dr. Charles Woffinden from the School of Mathematics and Physics]. "While the present system is far from practical, it demonstrates the possibility of communicating using a method that ordinary physical barriers cannot block." Professor Andrew White said the biggest limitation to future gravity-based communication was its slow speed. "Our elevator was snail-paced -- it's from the 1950s -- so our experiment transmitted just 1 bit per minute, meaning it took an hour to send a single word," White said.
 
"The speed of gravity communication would come down to how big the mass is, how fast you can move it and the sensitivity of the detector. Our experiment used a classical gravity sensor, but our modeling indicates that quantum sensors could, with rather ambitious assumptions, support ranges of up to about 500 meters (1,640 feet) and data rates of around 15 bits per minute."
